utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We continue to sit under the provisions of section 15 bis in the absence of Judge Kwon. A moment of indulgence, please from the witness. The just a few matters to deal with as far as the Prosecution is concerned. I talk to you, Mr. Tieger, but I don't think it's going to be for you to actually resolve these issues. There's some illegible documents, 65 ter number 09163 and 16923 are partially illegible in their English original version. Can you organise the upload of clearer versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: There's a video, 65 ter 40108 is not been uploaded into e-court. Perhaps the Prosecution could ensure that a -- that is corrected. And there's been a wrong video provided to the Chamber although the 92 ter notification tells us that the Prosecution is tendering 65 ter 40387, the CD provided in the notifications appendix bears 65 ter number 40287. Perhaps that could be amended as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellency. Good morning to all. Good morning, Dr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I wish to ask you something. I'm always prepared to work as hard as necessary, especially to make things easier for our witness, however, I wanted to ask you whether it would be possible for us not to work on the 21st of November or to work on the Friday after the 21st of November, because this is a major Christian holiday that my family has been celebrating for the past 800 years, the St. Archangel Michael. If that would be possible, I would kindly ask you to rule on that in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So what you are asking is that we don't sit on the 21st but we do sit on the 25th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If necessary to make up for that time, we can work on the 25th, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I can imagine that the schedule having been set out for some time that other things may be, as it were, organised already by individuals concerned for the 25th. But the Chamber will consider your request in good time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, at the very outset I wanted to check what I'm going to say right now is all right with you, namely different documents of a political nature or other documents from that time, once they get into the courtroom with regard to this criminal matter, legal criminal matter, when they move into a courtroom from the political arena, they call for making meanings more defined and focusing on definitions of various kinds, so would you please understand that, and please do not feel that you are personally being attacked or that the UN is being attacked, if I ask where things come from and if I ask for them to be very precisely defined. Is that all right with you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to say something that is on the record from all the previous six trials with regard both to the testimony that is called my witness statement and my presence. The entire document, which in the narrative that you have now are copiously documented by references in footnotes refer to documents which are in nature United Nations documents. The Prosecutor was allowed access, not by me, but by the United Nations, in the archives of the United Nations. They selected all of those documents for the purposes they wanted in this trial. Secondly, they obtained clearance from the United Nations to table these documents and because by the selections they made those documents were authored by me, my presence was to authenticate and validate those documents. The narrative that is being called the "amalgamation" is an accurate narrative with regard to those documents. And finally, Your Honour, the time those documents were prepared as indicated in all the previous trials, was not really for the court. They were intended for reporting up the UN chain. Therefore, they have to be taken in the context in which they were written. I hope I've clarified that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Dr. Kirudja. That's a useful and, if I may say so, I suspect understood clarification as far as Dr. Karadzic is concerned, certainly as far as the Chamber is concerned. No doubt, he will proceed to cross-examine you upon that basis. If there are any difficulties that arise where you feel that you are in professional difficulties as a result of your activities and duties in respect to the UN, then you will need to tell us so we can determine accordingly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Dr. Kirudja. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First, I would like it to deal with the most sensitive topic and that the question of the fate of civilians in Bosnia Krajina, or rather, the municipalities that you dealt with, especially Bosanski Novi, et cetera. In paragraph 41 of your amalgamated statement -- Doctor, do you need to have that before you, the statement itself? Maybe it would be better if you had a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's okay with you, and if it's okay with the Court, if he refers to a paragraph like, say, paragraph 41, which he has just referred to, perhaps it might be sufficient just to flash it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We attempt to restrict what comes on to the monitor and to which those matters which are germane to the question, so we leave it to the staff to use their expertise in this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can provide Mr. -- Dr. Kirudja with a hard copy of his amalgamated witness statement if he wants to have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It may well be of continuing help throughout the proceedings. Unless there are any objections from the Defence, which I doubt in the circumstances, please, that's very useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I now ask you to focus your attention on paragraph 41 where you described how the mayor of Dvor informed you about the wishes of the mayor of Bosanski Novi who confirmed to him that Muslims, or rather, people, who wished to leave Bosanski Novi wished to do so voluntarily, and we see the entire paragraph now, don't we? Did they inform you that before that the Serb authorities of the Bosnian Krajina, or rather, these municipalities, made an offer to the effect that civilians be moved in depth into Republika Srpska out of the areas close to combat zones to Doboj and elsewhere, whereas the Muslim negotiators refused all of that, they just asked to go to Croatia and Europe?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paragraph that Dr. Karadzic draws my attention to, paragraph 41, has a straightforward understanding of what it says, that, one, the mayor of Dvor -- and for the Court's understanding, Dvor is a municipality across the river from Bosnia, and it fell into one of those municipalities that were in Sector North in the jurisdiction of United Nations as a protected area and in a territory recognised as part of Croatia. That's Dvor. The mayor being discussed, Pasic, is a mayor of Bosanski Novi across the river into Bosnia. The paragraph says and summarises a sequence of events that result into the conclusion in the paragraph that the mayor of Dvor, speaking on behalf of the mayor of Bosanski Novi, asks that refugees coming from Bosanski Novi transition into the UNPA and should be allowed to get out and they were doing so voluntarily. The paragraph -- the word is put in quotes. Now, Dr. Karadzic is talking about whether they informed me something else. No, they informed me exactly what the paragraph is saying. Nothing more, nothing less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kirudja. In paragraph 43, you describe what happened. You say that you noticed that the mayor and his associates sounded very authentic when speaking of the aspirations of the Serbs and then you asked them, how they, as Serbs, could speak with assurance about the aspirations of Muslims without a single Muslim representative being present. Then they replied -- actually, we all see this paragraph, don't we? That they can arrange for you to meet with Muslim representatives. Further down, you say that they called Pasic, the mayor of Bosanski Novi, and that Pasic was prepared to talk to you but you declined to speak with him but they still encouraged you to establish contact with Pasic. After all, would it not have been a good idea for you to have spoken to the mayor of Bosanski Novi? Would that have been useful for you to see exactly what kind of information he had?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Karadzic. It is a summary, that paragraph, of events that transpired. The decline to speak to Mayor Pasic, if you look carefully, Dr. Karadzic, is to speak to him on the telephone. Actually, Mayor Borojevic was holding the telephone and saying Mayor Pasic is on line, could you please speak to him. Now, I had just arrived in the office of Mayor Borojevic to discuss what I had considered normal United Nations peacekeeping matters inside the UNPA. I'm being given a telephone to speak to a mayor outside the jurisdiction of the United Nations mission about a matter that sounded to me, while very interesting but urgent but difficult to deal with, so the decline was not a matter that I would want to discuss on the telephone and therefore I declined to speak. Not because, as the question posed by Dr. Karadzic may imply that I didn't want to speak to him. Actually, I considered the matter quite serious, and I declined to deal with it that way. But the paragraph ends by noting we soon later, we met with Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, Dr. Kirudja, that Mayor Pasic had many reasons to be anxious in view of the concentration of civilians, Muslim civilians, and the presence of elements that were out of control, paramilitary groups, et cetera, and he had reasons for fearing that something might happen to him? Does that sound reasonable to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are speaking chronologically, at that point when I got notice that he would want to speak to me, I didn't have all the details of what might be behind the request to speak. Therefore, I couldn't agree or disagree with Dr. Karadzic that that was what was motivating him. It took me days and weeks to interrogate the issue, and as the narrative told several paragraphs after the one he has drawn our attention to indicates, we came to some conclusions about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I believe that before you assumed your duties in the Balkans, or rather, the UNPAs, you were briefed about the country that you were going to and the situation that you would find there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is reasonable to assume that we did get briefs of the country that we -- the mission was being said to operate in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do forgive me for asking this, however, on the basis of our experience, it seems that many people came with certain prejudices, preformed views, that we had to clarify over time. During these briefings, did you take a particular position in terms of what was going on in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to clarify for the Court. While understanding the intention of the question and my mission that we did get briefing, I would like to clarify to the Court what kind of briefings we got. The briefings, as always, in the United Nations, is about the nature of the mission, the Security Council document which enabled the mission, you are supposed to be familiar with what those documents say. Those documents are limited in purpose and content to what the mission is about. If Dr. Karadzic is thinking of a broader context than that, then of course not. The UN will not brief beyond its own purposes and its own intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I may assume that you had not known, for instance, that the Muslim side in Bosnia-Herzegovina, already in June 1991, established its own ethnic council for national security, and a subcommittee for the Una region that bordered with your area. The Una zone would imply that it's around the Una river. Did you know that they started doing that already in spring 1991?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Dr. Karadzic, that specific detail wouldn't have been known to me before coming into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you observed that preparations and war aid was underway from the Muslims who lived throughout Europe, they were getting together and they were preparing equipment and personnel for helping. You refer to that in paragraph 25 of your statement. Could you please focus on that now. You were informed that about 1.600 people wanted to return to Velika Kladusa, Bosanska Krupa and Otoka. Could you please take a look at that document. Then you say that they had been gathered at the stadium of a particular football club? Do you remember having observed that? Do you know that that was quite a strong brigade, rather two light brigades given our situation that wanted to go back to Bosnia to fight?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, two elements I pick up from the long comment from Dr. Karadzic. One, the word "observed preparations" and "war aid underway from the Muslims who lived throughout Europe." Obviously I didn't observe that, since it was, if I understand the comment correctly, something happening before I arrived. If that's the question, then obviously I didn't observe it. Second, I'm drawn to the content of paragraph 25. The paragraph has moved both in time and place, the content of the paragraph, rather. They are talking about 1600 outside Karlovac, nowhere near Bosanski Novi. We are talking about Karlovac. The time is 1992, the earlier comment is talking about previous events. If I understand Dr. Karadzic correctly, he is linking them this way. The people who are in the Ilovac football field in Karlovac wanted to return into the area which Dr. Karadzic is referring our attention to, yes, I observed that because I went to see them and to talk to them. Secondly, Dr. Karadzic is correct, I was told, not by the people themselves, but by the general who commanded the 10th Corps, when I relayed their requests to him, he said, no, we are not going to allow them to cross over the UNPA from Karlovac into Bosnia because they are trained fighters and we won't allow them. Then to that extent I think the statement is correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just presented the content of paragraph 26, so I'm not going to dwell on it. Did you know that on that very same day, the 29th of April, the day that you referred to in paragraph 26, that purchases were being made through the Croatian ministry but for the Muslim side, actually, ministries, Croatian ministries of defence, the interior and so on and other organisations in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make things easier for you, let us have a look at D401.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document coming from the Islamic Association of Croatia and Slovenia and it talks about receipt of money for the purchase of weapons to be dispatched to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Kirudja, I was going to ask you whether you knew what the links between these organisations, Islamic organisations, throughout Europe that were led by Dr. Fatih Ali Hasanein, and the other organisations in the arming of people for the needs of the Bosnian war?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know their links.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that this could reach Bosnia and Herzegovina from Croatia either through the UNPA zones or across the Sava river or from the other side, from the Adriatic coast?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the question is was there a possibility that could happen, as opposed to did that, of course, I had to admit there is a possibility. Things could move that way. Not that I knew they were moving, but I would admit there were possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it have been useful for your reports had we, for instance, informed you of this on time? Would that have been useful in order to get the full picture?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I ask questions or respond to them. My answer to this would have been a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I think if you need to ask a question to clarify the question, although it's not something that we encourage, if it means that you are going to be able to answer the question more efficiently, I think perhaps you ought to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm reading the question as Dr. Karadzic posing the hypothetical question that they would have reported to us. They never reported to us, nor did they actually report to us, so would that have been a difference? That's the question I'll ask. What difference it would have made if they reported to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Cutting through it, I suppose, Dr. Karadzic, what you mean is that would the UN have been assisted by that knowledge in having a broader understanding of the picture had you made such reports. Was that what you were getting at?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, it is well known, would you agree, that the Serb side was insufficiently savvy, both in informing the media and the UN, and this was precisely the gist of my question and it was what Judge Morrison formulated so well?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thank you for that clarification, Dr. Karadzic, and my comment on it was that I wouldn't quite characterise the Serb as "insufficiently savvy." My experience was in the areas where they controlled or they were the authorities in control of life in that area, specifically say the UNPA, they were actually in a position to select what they wanted us to know and what they didn't want us to know. Not that they were insufficiently savvy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether timely information on these operations to arm the Bosnian Muslims through various religious organisations at the time of the embargo and the sanctions, would that have been of use to the UN as information?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm confused about the issue of embargo and sanctions. I'm not aware how that issue played out in the situation. Could you clarify a little bit more, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if you recall, in 1991 already there was a ban on the imports of any kind of war material and weapons into any of the republics of the former Yugoslavia. Now, do you recall that this was a step taken by the UN and published in the resolution?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say I am aware of the events that went one year or so before the mission was established. Yes, I am aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So in the midst of this embargo on the imports of weapons, what I'm trying to say is that many international organisations funneled huge quantities of weapons, mainly via Croatia and Slovenia, weapons meant for arming the Muslim side in Bosnia and Herzegovina, were you aware of that? And in that context, would it have been useful for the UN to have timely information on what was going on?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question makes me want to clarify to the Court some of the assumptions we were given to understand about the context of the mission, specifically when this mission called UNPROFOR was set up by the United Nations, it was set up in rather unusual experiment if I might use that word, though the UN will cringe that they do anything under experiment. I'm a retired person now and I can call it that. They set up a mission on the understanding that the people who fought in Croatia, the areas of Croatia that were taken, had not been through fighting. They were not ready actually and there was no formula for a peaceful settlement. So the mission was set up to freeze where they were in the fighting, hoping they can be talked into, one, not to resuming any fighting, and ending the fighting they had. And on that understanding, the assumption, strange as it may sound to you, that the mission would not be placed entirely in the area where they fought but would be placed in an area the UN thought was peaceful; therefore, the headquarters of the mission was selected to be Sarajevo. And the military logistics battalions, of all places, had been located in Banja Luka. Why? Because that was "peaceful." So the assumption was the area that Dr. Karadzic is talking about being armed was assumed to be peaceful. When I drove from Sector West to Topusko, an area in Croatia, I drove through Bosnia. Two military people drove me through Bosnia because it was more peaceful. So the entire premise was Bosnia and Herzegovina was peaceful, and Croatia, the parts that are taken, were not peaceful. So for me to hear now that they were preparing for war, I can only say it took me up to May to discover, indeed, something was not peaceful over there. And we found it the hard way. I was in the convoy with the force commander, General Nambiar through Bihac when they were stopped by armed people inside the peaceful area. Now, I've taken this long to explain a simple point that the area that I'm listening to Dr. Karadzic being armed as -- as being armed we had assumed it was peaceful and it was going to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know -- were you informed that even before your arrival, the fighting from in Croatia was spilling over into Bosnia and that was shooting from the Croat side into Bosnia and that there were Bosnian victims very early on already in July and all the way through the beginning of the war in Bosnia itself?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: July of which year, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly take a look at D1911. It's a police report from July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at this document. Mention is made of Bosanski Novi, Dubica, Gradiska and Srbac, these are territories bordering on Croatia and it says there that -- that forces were being grouped there, that there was shooting, that automatic weapons were being brought in from the territory of Croatia. On the 26th and the 27th of June there was incessant fighting which lasted over two hours and so on and so forth. Now, were you when you were briefed, were you also informed that you could run into this and that the war was spilling over across the border with Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask the date of July is 1991. The mission was not authorised until a year later in April, 1992. I have also taken a little of your time, Your Honour, to say the understanding was the war among these parties had not been ended, yet the United Nations Security Council decided in good faith, it was like a prayer you would say, a Hail Mary, that we are going to go in there and help make sure things don't get worse than they are and hopefully better. Yes, it was understood this war had not ended, which explains why a UN mission like UNPROFOR would be headed by a soldier. Most UN missions are not headed by a soldier. They are headed by a civilian when there is a peace formula. This mission was headed at the top by General Satish Nambiar in recognition that there was still fighting going on. I even experienced it on my way into the area. There were smouldering tanks and cocked guns at crossing points. Yes, if the statement is that there was fighting, that was understood, there was fighting, but what I would like the Court to understand is that both governments that were signatory to this mission, the government in Belgrade and government in Zagreb had agreed they would end or hold the status quo; no more fighting. That was the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kirudja, my -- it was my intention to explore whether you had been informed in time that the crisis had begun in Bosnia much earlier, long before May 1992, and that for almost a year all these municipalities, including Bosanski Novi, were exposed to shells coming from the other side, that there was shooting, although the war had not officially broken out in Bosnia and Herzegovina yet. Would you agree with me that -- did you know how long these tensions were rising on the Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I appreciate that question from Dr. Karadzic in a different way. My responsibility was in a sector, the very sector bordering on these municipalities in Bosnia. My difficulties, and somewhere in this testimony you will find reference to it, my headquarters were convinced of their own assumption that that area was peaceful. My task was to tell them something they didn't expect and frankly didn't want to hear, that there was trouble. And you -- I forget which paragraph in here but maybe the counsel for Prosecution can refer to the paragraph where I'm being admonished that you are spending too much time telling us about this area. It took us a very short period to find out that there was trouble but I want to make also clear to the Court, it wasn't uniform trouble. It was selective trouble along that border because of the nature of those municipalities that Dr. Karadzic is talking about. In this report we are talking about, for purposes of explaining to the people we were reporting to, we had divided that border in two parts. One part is where the municipalities were controlled by the Serbs on both sides. And those were the municipalities in Kostajnica on the UNPA Dvor or across the other side in Bosanski Novi and the other municipalities named where the Serbs were in control on both sides. There were no trouble there. There was no difficulties there. Trouble starts when you go to the Velika Kladusa, Bosnia, Bosanska Krupa, Prijedor, these were Muslims controlled on one side and on the UNPA side the Serbs were there. That's where trouble was. So it wasn't a uniform trouble, it was a specific trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope you understand that I'm making a pause for interpretation. Now, I would like to thank you, Dr. Kirudja, for the clarification you've provided. However, irrespective of the fact that you had a mandate within the UNPA area, the Prosecution is hoping that with the help of your knowledge and your reports they will be able to also prove some events on the Bosnian side. That's why I'm asking you about this. Now, I would like to show you an intercept. True, this conversation was before you arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 03177.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will see from this intercept on the 31st of August, 1991, from the Croatian side Serbs were killed in Bosanski Novi by a sniper. My intention is to show the build-up of this crisis in Bosnia and to show that it did not just break out all of a sudden, but rather that it was very much under the influence of the war that was going on. Now, we will see that intercept in a moment and I will show you that on the 31st of August there was shooting on Bosanski Novi and people were getting killed there. Did anyone ever tell you that the war was spilling over and that there was a lot of shooting into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only came to the same conclusion that the war was spilling over, not at the time period, Dr. Karadzic, you take your reference, but after we arrived there, and a good part of my report was to document precisely that, that the war was spilling over the areas where the UN thought it has a mandate and establishing that mandate and changing or calling for change in that mandate. We made conscious effort to document that fact, even at the risk of me getting hand-slapped about it. Well, for want of a better word hand-slapped, being warned, that the UN has no mandate in those areas. But I had no option, nor was there any option left to me and other people, and I did say that in the strongest terms I could to the people that didn't want to listen in my headquarters. The people who were coming to us seeking refuge were not drawn by a mandate. There was a flag, a blue flag, flying where we were and they saw them or took the shortest route to that area. And they told us their story. And our duty was to tell that story. But I agree with Dr. Karadzic to the extent that the war was spilling over when we are looking at it. The dates where he is starting from, with obvious understanding, is dates that I couldn't authenticate since I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please take a look at the bottom of -- or the lower part of this intercept where Krajisnik is talking to me and he is telling me that two men were killed in a cafe by a sniper shooter from the other side of the river, from the Croatian side. If you have found this portion, we don't have to keep this on the screen anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, could this be admitted under the same conditions as those that apply to all intercepts that have been admitted so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that here we see that it is being said that there was a cold-blooded murder from the -- that occurred that was perpetrated from the other side of the river and that this had to have an effect on Bosanski Novi long before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately your wording, Dr. Karadzic is much too strong for me to authenticate. You are calling it a cold-blooded murder which is a judgement I couldn't corroborate too, since I'm just looking at this statement that something happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the third box from the bottom I say that this was a cold-blooded murder because that's how we saw it then. This was long before the war in Bosnia. But, all right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's an intercept, you asking it be MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as we've done so far with intercepts when admitting them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D1915, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, you testified in the Milosevic case, 65 ter 22681, and on page 15550 of 4th February 2003, of the transcript you said that Croatian forces violated the Vance Plan when they attacked Miljevac, the Miljevac plateau, do you recall saying that? And on the following page, the following two pages, you characterised Croatians as aggressors against an UNPA area, that this was something they were not allowed to do. Would you stand by this statement of yours from that period?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be more helpful for me to see the full statement since those are extracts from the statement. And, yes, the location being referred to I have a memory of. Of course I have testified to many things in six trials and it would just be helpful if I see the context in which reference is being made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, that would help.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no Serbian translation, we don't really need one now so we can just have the text in English. 15550. That should be the page number. And then 15556 and 15557. Can it be zoomed in. This is 14550 whereas we need 15550.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the Brdjanin trial, not the Milosevic trial. I see the examination by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One page further up. Can we scroll down now, please. We now see the answer, Dr. Kirudja's answer, a bit further down. The next page as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that this was a crisis and that the UNPAs were being attacked in September 1992 and do you also remember that at the same time in Banja Luka there was an armed rebellion, a mutiny, as it were, in my own army?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like for the Court now to place in context the earlier statement that I had said something about violation. It's clear we were talking about the Security Council report that came to that conclusion. It wasn't my conclusion, as you can see at the bottom, line 9. Mr. Milosevic was interrogating that report through me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The report effectively stands alone because it was the Security Council's report and it was one that you, like everyone else, simply received from the Security Council; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the crisis that we had in Banja Luka when there was this mutiny, this unit rebelled and there was a crisis in Banja Luka for about ten days?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, do you recall the month, year when this crisis occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 9th of September, 1993. The 9th of September up until the 17th of September there was this rebellion, mutiny. There was a total blockade of the city itself. I believe that you observed that and that you heard about it from your colleagues' reports or that it was in your reports?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Karadzic. The way we were organised to report and cover matters occurring in the area where the UN mission was deployed placed the area Dr. Karadzic is talking about under a person with my capacity and his name was Viktor Andreev. Those issues would have come through a report by Viktor Andreev based in Sarajevo. It wouldn't have come through me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The transcript is obviously -- it's been corrected now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please take a look at D192 [as interpreted] briefly. Let us see what the situation was in Bosanski Novi in mid-April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, did you know that at the time, or rather, during the period that preceded the Vance Plan for Croatia, that what happened en masse were sieges and attacks against JNA barracks in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had another understanding of what happened and the report itself makes reference to it. When we arrived under the Vance Plan at the early part of this narrative, you get a picture of what we were required to do in three parts. The first part involved the military part that said we need to take over where the warring parties had stopped, get them to lay down their arms, demobilise and take control. At that time the entire area which was my charge was under the 10th Corps of the JNA commanded by General Spiro Ninkovic. He did give us a good idea of the fighting that took place in that area prior to our arrival. My understanding is that when there is a fight, of course it can't be a one-sided fight, you receive and you give, but the balance of the fight was in favour of the 10th Corps to the point that he took pride on the report, the narrative that was used, Your Honour, that they took the war up to the edges where they wanted to go because they were able to do so. They considered and give up as impractical the idea of taking the war beyond the Mreznica and Kupa river short of Karlovac and Zepa. So my understanding of the fighting was pretty much a one-sided fight. And he said so himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kirudja. It would be interesting if we had enough time to hear all your views on that situation. However, I would like to read a paragraph out to you. All of this because I want us to see all the things that Mr. Pasic knew and what he was dealing with before he asked you for assistance, so please bear with me. This is a police report of the 16th of April, 1992. And the paragraph I'm reading out says: [As read] "However, the escalation of war conflicts. Constant aggression against units and barracks of the JNA in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as well as the presence of Croatian paramilitary forces, the HOS and the ZNG, in -- on the outskirts of the broader region accompanied by a lack of personal security of citizens and safety of their property as well as the economic collapse are all factors that blatantly reflect the possibility of an outburst of dissatisfaction and certainly an inter-ethnic conflict with catastrophic consequences." The sentence before all of this says that this has to do with the situation in Bosanski Novi. So this is my question now, Dr. Kirudja: Do you accept that the mayor of Novi, Bosanski Novi, Pasic, had to bear all of this on his shoulders June 1991, September 1991, sniping, shelling, killing of civilians, then further on it says that many mobilised persons who fought in Slavonia are coming back. I'm going to read out the previous paragraph to you as well: [As read] "This lack of balance is contributed to by the cessation of military conflicts as well as the arrival of UN peacekeepers in the areas of Banija and Western Slavonia where many mobilised citizens from the area of Bosanski Novi were stationed in JNA units." Do you agree that considerably before the UN arrived and before the crisis broke out in Bosanski Novi there were many things going on that prepared for that crisis?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, what the mayor was asking Novi had to bear in 1999 [sic] prior our arrival may well be what Dr. Karadzic says he had to bear. I don't know since I didn't witness it. That is entirely possible and then again, I wouldn't confirm or deny it. But when we arrived there, when he approached me, he began to tell a story of a period of time whose parts did not coalesce or didn't agree with each other, and the narrative you have takes you through that and one of that was you are telling us there are 5.000 people gathered in your town, the town where you are the mayor and they want to leave voluntarily. First question to him by me, why now? Why would people leave the comfort of their homes and seek shelter somewhere else? And why are you talking on their behalf with none of their representatives here for us to hear? Remember we are not challenging him. We are strangers. We don't know the facts. So the passport of that allegation falls apart because he says there's a new reality to the question why now, and I ask what reality? We have a new country called Republic of Serb -- Republika Srpska of BiH, and I say, pray, when did this start, I don't know, he says. So the Muslims won't swear allegiance. So then I say to him, so you are living together here comfortably and suddenly you want them to swear allegiance to a new thing? Yes, because it's the rule, he says. And I said to him, what rule? And he says, I don't know but it's called this. And then I say to him, and then what happened? We want them to disarm. And I said, you want them to disarm. Yes. Why would they want to be armed if everything is peaceful? Then the next shoe drops because they are being attacked by irregulars around us and whose irregulars, they can't be Muslims, no, but they are Serb irregulars. And the story went on. I, at a certain point, if what had happened there were tension before, he would have told me. We've been fighting for some time prior, this is what was going on. No, he didn't say that. He said they won't disarm and they won't swear allegiance to the new reality. So they have to leave. So then I say so they are not leaving voluntarily? And he says, not really. He agrees. They are not leaving voluntarily. Then I say to him, then why would people who don't want to swear allegiance, don't want to fight, why do they want to keep arms? And he says to me, and the report again does make that amply clear, says, no, because they are militarily weak. They can't really fight and they don't want to go to the other part, Western Bosnia controlled by the government of Izetbegovic. So the explanations given live and in the moment never went back to the past of tensions, so I wouldn't have known there were tensions nor did they even talk about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kirudja. Please focus on paragraph 48 of your statement where you describe the continuation of your conversation with Mr. Pasic. Mr. Pasic's position was that they were not to go or to go further to Republika Srpska. However, he informed you that Serb policemen were killed, a police patrol had been attacked, and that they were resolved to go but not just to any part of Bosnia, only to Western Europe. They didn't want to go anywhere in Bosnia regardless of whether it was under Serb or Muslim control. Were you informed that they wanted to leave Bosnia as such?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I was informed by the Serbs this is what the Muslims want to do. I wasn't informed by the Muslims. I was informed by the Serbs that this is what the Muslims want to do. I want to make that specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 50 you say that you asked them what was it that had changed in Bosanski Novi and for that reason I note that no one had informed you about how long the crisis had been going on, about when the crises started and when tensions went up in Bosanski Novi and in this entire border area. So I'm asking you now, did you know that the Muslim side from the end of April 1991 up until the beginning of April 1992 had over 150.000 armed men in the Patriotic League, that they had staffs, nine regional staffs and 103 municipal staffs, and that they were actively preparing for war against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know it then nor do I know it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And do forgive me for wishing for brief answers because I am afraid that we will not be able to deal with everything and I wouldn't want us to keep you here next week as well. I accept that that was our mistake, the fact that you were not sufficiently informed, but you do accept that Pasic's knowledge and experience up until the 27th of May when you met was rife with problems that you had been unaware of; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know all his problems when he came to speak to me, but he had specific ones that he came to speak to me about. Those are the removal of those 5.000 people. Well, this needs to be specified from the point of view of criminal law, so please understand me. In paragraph 77 of your statement you spoke about the 6th of July when Mr. Pasic sent you a letter. Please take a look at that paragraph. Pasic signed the letter and he said that Muslims and people from other ethnic backgrounds were voluntarily leaving their homes and were seeking assistance to leave the municipality. May I ask you this now, Dr. Kirudja, do you agree that there is not a single army in the world that could tolerate being shot in the back by their very own people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Totally agree. There is a responsibility that authorities in power have, and one of them is to restore order in the legal jurisdictions in which they operate. If that's the question, I understand that, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 46 you describe your dilemma in terms of why people wish to leave their homes, and you describe what Mr. Pasic said to you. Now I would like to complete the picture. The front lines are far away from Bosanski Novi and you know what the front line or conflict line was like in Bosnia. However, in the villages of Bosanski Novi there was a military organisation of the Muslims that was attacking and killing small police patrols. This led to a reaction. Not on the part of the legal authorities, but organs that were out of control, or rather, groups that were out of control that then took their revenge and exerted pressure against the Muslims? Do you find that understandable? Is this what Mr. Pasic said to you exactly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I want to make this very clear, that was not understandable to me, not then, not now. There were too many conflicting things that the mayor said to me. I want -- in the earlier paragraph 77, Dr. Karadzic notes that despite all those exchanges, despite all those discussions in an attempt for me to understand it, despite the fact that in my presence he accepts that they were not voluntary, they were not doing this on their own, he still writes the letter claiming they were doing it voluntarily. No, nothing was understandable in the way it was being presented at that time. But one thing was being clear, they were driven to do this. They wanted to do this and if I stood in their way, they ask who is my superior since we can't get through to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now we have to spell this out in very specific terms, Dr. Kirudja. When it says that someone was forced to leave, although they did not wish to leave but they do decide to leave nevertheless, I would like us to shed more light on this. Was it developments as such that compel the Muslims to do that as well as pressure exerted by elements that were out of control, or was this done by Mr. Pasic? In paragraph 77 and in paragraph 46, is it not clearly shown that the regular forces have nothing to do with this, that no one wants to pressure the Muslims in any way? However, the pressure comes from developments as such, how events unravelled. So they were not forced by the authorities but by the developments as such, as they unravelled?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to make it clear that, Dr. Karadzic, we understood that. We have in the narrative said so, that Pasic was telling us it wasn't the force, the regular forces. We do reflect that. But he is also telling us there were irregular forces doing it and those irregular forces were in his jurisdiction. The question arises, if you are a regular force of law, you make no distinction between some of your citizens doing irregular things, but this time you focus on the one on the receiving end of those irregular forces. That's what the implication of that statement is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Dr. Kirudja, the very fact that they were irregular and that Mr. Pasic is issuing orders to the regular Territorial Defence to resubordinate them, to control them, to disarm them, to disband them speaks in itself of the fact that they were not under his control, that makes them irregular because they do not have a command above them. On the other hands they were the regular forces, the regular police going to those villages, arming Muslim policemen and charging them with taking care of the people, protecting the people. So the regular police, the regular forces are under Pasic's control and they behave in a regular manner. The irregulars are out of control. Anybody's control. Do you agree that this very notion of being out of control means that they are out of control?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, if that was what you were explaining, Mr. Karadzic, it would have been a different understanding. He wasn't asking the irregulars to disarm. He wasn't asking the irregulars to swear allegiance to his authority and do the right thing. He was asking -- or rather, he was saying, "I'm required to get the swearing of allegiance from the people in the receiving end of these irregulars." By a new authority he called it a new reality. If what Dr. Karadzic is explaining was explained at that time, we would have queried why you were unable to do something about it. We never discussed that. What he was talking about was they don't want to do it, they can't live with us, therefore they must leave. The narrative over a period, it's not a single session. Towards the end the narrative says once you understand we can't live together, the Serbs and the Muslim, everything will be solved. Not about lawlessness, not about irregular, not about breakdown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We'll take a break now. We'll adjourn. We'll resume sitting again at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, I have to ask you to be as brief as possible in your answers because we don't have enough time and there is a host of documents that we have to go through. Now, as far as your last answer was concerned, this answer that you gave and your position behind it, is that based on the fact that Pasic did not order the disbanding and disarming of paramilitary units, Serb paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate the request by Dr. Karadzic for me to be brief, and I endeavour to be brief. I also note for the record his questions are pretty complex. If they were simpler, they will get a simpler answer. Nevertheless, we'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I think in fencing that's known as touche.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question about Mr. Pasic's request to us and how we saw it was not that of trying to make him do or not do something. We wanted to understand, Dr. Karadzic, what it is he wanted us to do. It's that simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Dr. Kirudja, we showed through other witnesses to the Trial Chamber various orders issued by Mr. Pasic, orders to regular forces to take measures against irregular forces. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I wouldn't be aware of Mr. Pasic's dealings with other people, interlocutors. I certainly wouldn't be aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, these were orders issued by Mr. Pasic and orders issued by the Municipal Assembly, the parliament, at the proposal of the Serb Democratic Party to take severe action and disband these units. That was an order and did you know this because your last reply before the break contained an implication that Pasic should have taken care of the victims and not paramilitary units. Were you aware that Pasic took very severe measures and attempted severe measures against paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Pasic as not reticent in telling me what he had in mind. He engaged me over a period of time with a single-mind objective. I have recounted that and it is reflected in the narrative. At no time did the issue of whether or not he was trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Dr. Kirudja, my only question is do you know -- and I just ask my question based on your reply before the break. Do you know that Mr. Pasic and the municipal authorities issued orders to the Territorial Defence to disband and hamper the operations of the Serb paramilitary units? Can you just answer that question.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. He never spoke of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that in addition to Serb paramilitary units in Novi Grad municipality and the villages in question, there was -- there was operational a secret Muslim military unit which also had a lot of weapons?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that there was a train prepared for these Muslims to take the Muslims from the areas, endangered areas to Banja Luka, that they refused, returned, went back to their villages and remained there for another 17 days?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is covered in one paragraph in my narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 23028, please. We don't need the version in Serbian other than for the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But would you agree that this is a communication from the High Commission for Refugees and he reports on an incident on the evening of 7th of July when they received information that 79 refugees were outside of the police station asking assistance to cross to Croatia, and that in the second paragraph it say that they did leave the police station and returned to Bosanski Novi. And then in paragraph 4 we see that they met -- they had another meeting with the Muslims, that it took -- that it lasted three hours and they were able to interview family members, or rather, families who represented these Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see in paragraph 7 it says that the crisis committee of Bosanski Novi addresses a letter to civil affairs in Sector North, that was your unit, wasn't it? And informed you that 1233 persons had applied to the authorities for permission to leave and then it says that those who did not have their own means of transportation would be provided for transportation by the municipality. Those who have their own cars would leave in their own cars. Then in paragraph 8 we see that there was a meeting between the mayor and then towards the bottom it says that these 1300 families who fulfilled the criteria are not the same individuals, those 5.000 Muslims who were -- who left in a convoy at the end of May and who managed to escape and so on and so forth, and those routes that they had taken were no longer open. Do you know, Dr. Kirudja, that not a single certificate on the change of ownership was ever actually implemented.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 10 where it says that the deputy mayor stressed that he wouldn't do anything about the UNPROFOR. And then please take a look at what you here attributed to Mr. Pasic, toward the end of paragraph 11, it says: [In English] [As read] "When I asked them to confirm that the mayors of Bosanski Novi and Banja Luka had been on the news in Banja Luka TV stating that Muslims and Serbs could no longer live together, they said it was not the mayor but the chief of the crisis committee in Banja Luka, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin." [Interpretation] Can you remember that Mr. Pasic -- can you remember that it was ever reported that it was Mr. Pasic who said that they couldn't live together? Were you aware of this clarification, that this was something that was attributed to Pasic but it was not in fact Pasic's position.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I get the idea that this testimony is contrasted with the narrative and there is some contrast being drawn, that the narrative said somewhere Pasic said something. I don't know that and if I have to comment on it, I would comment on a specific paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is paragraph 84 of -- referred to in Dr. Kirudja's statement at paragraph 84. And it's also an associated exhibit so it should have an exhibit number by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P3840, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we still have this document before us --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, footnote 211.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, while we still have this document before us, would you accept that there is a difference whether -- when something is said by the president of the municipality where all three ethnicities are supposed to live or when those words were pronounced by a member of parliament where it would refer to the entire population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if it is Brdjanin speaking, he is speaking about the transformation of the entire republic. If these were, however, the words of Pasic, then your interpretation would be correct. To be more specific, maybe I can help. Do you know that there was a conference before the war started on the transformation of Bosnia into three republics?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I will put it to you now, we accepted that Bosnia and Herzegovina could leave Yugoslavia under those conditions that were promoted by the European community, and Brdjanin was a deputy and he could accept those. So did you know that this proposal was accepted by the Assembly and that it was that this official proposal by the European Union was accepted?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry for interrupting but I just wanted to make the record clear, on page 34, line 21, Mr. Karadzic says as part of his question and then please take a look at what you here attributed to Mr. Pasic towards the end of paragraph 11 and it's not -- this witness isn't the author of this document that we are looking at on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Excellency, but Dr. Kirudja said in his reply something that did not find a way into his reports, in other words, that Mr. Pasic had told him that they could no longer go on living together. And here we see a UNHCR document which says that there were such rumours but it was clarified that it wasn't Pasic who said those words, but Brdjanin, and then I asked Dr. Kirudja whether he knew that Mr. Brdjanin was involved in the work of this conference that was supposed to produce three republics, the outcome of which was to be these three different republics, and that Brdjanin was authorised to speak of those things whereas Pasic was not. Now I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P3840, Your Honours. It's part of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes the procedure of the court and what you call a document from who, from different people is not always familiar to me. This document is authored by UNHCR. I'm entirely familiar with it because the author used to occupy a room in my office and it's been tendered in some of these footnotes as a Prosecution -- in the footnotes. So I wanted that clarification that when it says something and what the narrative summarises, the narrative is the summary. It's not the document from which the information being discussed came from. Narratives, by nature, condense it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Dr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, you did know that some Serb paramilitary units were disarmed; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 65 ter 23027, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3819, Your Honours, part of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your dispatch? Is this a document produced by you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the first page, please. We don't need the Serb version. Can we have the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that this document from the UNHCR were forwarded by you through your own channels to other authorities and that they related to the 5.000 inhabitants in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the document on the monitor right now I recognise, and has my name on it. I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the third page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the second half of the first paragraph. There you are mentioned and it says that you participated in a meeting with the mayor of Dvor and it also says that there were other members of the local government and then it goes on to say that on the 28th of May, the mayor of Bosanski Novi, Radomir Pasic, and his associate Palija visited you, and then in paragraph 3, it says that the request from Bosanski Novi was essentially a proposal that their police and Krajina police escort a group of 5.000, 5.000 Muslims, to the border of Croatia from where UNPROFOR should take over and escort them to the border of Slovenia and then on to Austria and Germany.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, let's take a look at paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But before that, do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the document to be from the same source I referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see paragraph 6, please. No, that's not the correct page. The previous page, please. This is chapter, or item 6 but not paragraph 6, so can we see the sixth paragraph. Please show the entire paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see here that this describes what Rade Palija reported, that they felt insecure, that they went to the authorities seeking help. They asked the authorities to help them to leave and then that there was a convoy of 5.000 people that was formed, that they wanted to leave to Austria and Germany where they had relatives and then in order to help them, the Bosanski Novi police and the Krajina police agreed to escort them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]Now, can we see the next page. And while we wait for that, Dr. Kirudja, are you aware of an agreement that was signed on the 22nd of May, 1992, an agreement between the three warring parties in Bosnia under the auspices of the UNHCR, according to which all the parties have the response -- are duty-bound to escort convoys of people who wanted to leave and cross over to another territory?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically that agreement of the three parties, no. I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see here it says that the Bosanski Novi authorities suggested that they leave and go to other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina where there were Muslim majorities but they refused because they were afraid they would be mobilised and for the same reason they did not want to enter Croatia alone. So in addition to the offer to go to Banja Luka or Doboj, they were also offered the possibility of crossing over to the Muslim territory but they declined all of those offers and they wanted to leave Bosnia as a whole. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only I was aware of that, it's reflected severally in the narrative that you have on my side, that very statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now take a look at the next paragraph where it says war had reached Bosanski Novi, the war that had started on the 6th of April in Bosnia, and it says here that within the last 15 to 20 days, the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina had reached Bosanski Novi, and that there were -- there was a certain amount of pressure from uncontrolled Serbian groups.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The same paragraph before the -- above number 5, chapter 5, within the last -- [In English] "... within the last 15, 20 days ..."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, if we go further down, we see that it says, the mayor: [In English] [As read] "... The mayor wanted to stress Serbian protection of these Muslims, some had even been taken into Serbian houses for protection in Serbian villages. Security at Blagaj was said to be provided by civil police and military police of the Army of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. Did you know that the official Serbian authorities did everything they could to protect these Muslims and if you look at paragraph 6, you see that they also organised meetings. There were meetings between the SDA and the SDS, we see it in that paragraph, where they discussed -- where they reached an agreement that all paramilitary groups should be disarmed and so on and so forth. Was that something that you were aware of too?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Court will note the narrative verbatim repeats those points. It's not that the security was provided. It says, "We are telling you the security was provided." Neither the author of that document nor our narrative says we know about security being provided. It says we are informed that the security is being informed [sic]. Two very different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is sufficient, Dr. Kirudja, that you had that information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the top we see that you were informed that some Serbian paramilitary groups had been disarmed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can we see chapter 9 or item 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where you inquired about the relevant, or rather, legitimate Muslim representatives. You were provided two names of people you could get in touch with. Now, do you know that Sifet Barjaktarevic was a leader and organiser of the paramilitary organisation of Muslims there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that because I never actually met them. My narrative says I didn't meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In any case, the Serbs recommended the two, that you should speak to the two of them; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, and I declined because I had learnt that the Serbs had imprisoned both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Shouldn't you have talked to them all the more so because of that specifically?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because of the subject. The subject was I want to know the true intentions of the Muslims. For that reason, I need a source that is not encumbered one way or the other to get the true intentions of the Muslims. I didn't think these two would lead me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 2303.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, Mr. Karadzic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 23030.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is a letter by the UNHCR to Mr. Pasic. Here we can see who was contacted and who sent their representatives. In the third paragraph, we can see again that the Serbs mention the names of Sifet Barjaktarevic and Fikret Hamzic as the people who could speak on behalf of the Muslim community. The mayor is being asked to set up a meeting with Muhamedagic and representatives of the local Red Cross or Merhamet. It goes on to say that the UNHCR is unwilling to take part in a new influx of refugees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this letter, its context and the circumstances under which it was written and its full intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next they ask to meet Mr. Muhamedagic. Do you know how they learned of that name?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To repeat to the Court, this letter is from the same source in my office with UNHCR mandate. It's a source that was always welcomed to my meetings. He knew everything that took place earlier. He knew about the two names, but there was a division of mandate and responsibility so he took his line, discussed with me, and this letter was the result.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this, Dr. Kirudja, with regard to this letter: Is it correct that you presumed that in Bosanski Novi the situation was quiet and within the ordinary as well as the authorities were in control? Did you presume that the authorities had their territory under control?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter chronologically comes towards the tail end from the first day we met in Dvor being requested to participate in the 5.000 people transit, to the point where we declined participation. This letter comes towards the end of that entire process. It cannot presume things were other than tense with the possibility that 5.000 people were being asked to leave their homes. It couldn't presume that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, do you have any proof that they were asked to do that, or was it the way I put it, which is that they asked a permission from the authorities to leave? Can you actually prove that it was the authorities who told them to leave, or was it the other way around?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire narrative is given in very simple sequence at the end of which the narrative says we came to the inescapable conclusion the people are not leaving voluntarily. It wasn't us who was confirming that, it is the people from Bosanski Novi that came to my office plus other offices upon questioning admitting to us, no it wasn't, and they give the reasons that are contained in the narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall we go back to where I started, Your Honour? I can relate the whole thing again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the witness has already explained that to us. It seems unnecessary for him to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at paragraph 44 then, Dr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is your conclusion: [In English] "After the meeting I concluded ..." [Interpretation] This was your conclusion, therefore, and no one ever told you that they were told to leave by the authorities, they were driven out by the events and a feeling of insecurity. Where did you report that the authorities actually accepted this position that they were telling the people who leave? Other than that, this is a mere conclusion of yours.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not. The paragraphs preceding that conclusion itemise answers to specific questions put on Bosanski Novi authorities and their answers put in quotes, not as conclusion, but as a direct statement; yes, we admit they are not leaving voluntarily. Why? Because they won't sign allegiance. They would not disarm. And we had a schedule in another paragraph showing what we did from the 6th of May to the 11th of May. It is all detailed there. Dr. Karadzic is correct when he reads I was left with no other option but conclude they were not leaving voluntarily. That is not a conclusion from -- or lacking in the events leading to it. That's a conclusion that falls to hand as those events are narrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, let me remind you the issue of signing loyalty oaths pertained only to the policemen who were given a possibility to work for the MUP of the RS. Given the fact that the RS was a newly formed state, everyone was asked to sign such an oath, including Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, because they had to state that they would abide by the law in the performance of their duties. In other words, ordinary people were not asked to sign such loyalty oaths; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I note that as Dr. Karadzic's comment and I let it stand. It's not my comment. It's not my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it your comment then that civilians were expected to sign loyalty oaths?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we were meeting them on a day-to-day basis, escaping from that area. And they were not Serbs. They were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
