utterances.text: In other words, your source of information was the Muslim refugees; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly, yes. The other source were the officials that came to see us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you show us where it was confirmed to you that civilians were expected to sign allegiance? Where in your statement? Do you have a document which would confirm that some civilians were expected to sign loyalty oaths if they were not civil servants?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a huge testimony given over a long period of time that we reported about refugees coming to our office being debriefed and recorded in meeting with us is part of that testimony. Exactly where it is, I can't tell you right now, Your Honour. It is there though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kirudja, let us be precise, did those refugees accept to be returned to Bosnia or did they wish to go further afield to Europe?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was different answers from different human beings. People go where they know others, so some will say where they have relatives, they have friends, it varied. But they were leaving. More importantly, some surprised us. Some had signatures that they will not return. It was a requirement you sign that you are not even coming back into your own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Save for what you were told by the refugees who did not wish to be repatriated, do you have any other circumstances which will testify to that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I got to go back to something I said earlier at the beginning of this. My testimony is not an affidavit to this court. My testimony is a compilation of the events that were happening as they were happening at that time for a different purpose. Prosecutor saw it fit to put together that information. So it's not that kind of testimony that Dr. Karadzic is interrogating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kirudja. However, this is a criminal matter, and I have to be precise to the last detail. I assert that it wasn't as you were told by the refugees, and that their statements were the result of their wish not to be repatriated. Is it so or is it not so? Was there such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that's a very difficult question. You are asking the witness to say what was in somebody else's mind. What he can say is what he was told, and if he was told it by enough people, whether he came to believe it. But asking what was in their minds was, with great respect, more a question for a psychiatrist than a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Let's look, then, at what you said at paragraph 79.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There you provide an answer to Judge El Mahdi's question concerning the SDS. Towards the end of the paragraph, it reads: [In English] "Even with that warning, they seemed not to be able or willing to stop the process. In other words, they did appear to have all the signs of being driven to undertake this and the only way to mind they could be driven is they were acting on instructions under a policy drawn by somebody and since they identified themselves as SDS or members of the militia or what they called, for better terminology, new reality going on and that reality called Republic of Serbia, it was, towards the end, inescapable for me to conclude they were acting under policy or instructions." [Interpretation] First of all, let's discuss a detail which appears here. You probably did not mean to say Serbia, but Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Secondly, here again you arrive at a conclusion. Did you ever attend an SDS meeting or did you ever see any documents which would make you draw that particular conclusion? Believe me, you can answer this with a simple yes or no and it would be much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like nothing better than to oblige and give you a yes or no. You phrased it that I can't. It's not a yes or no. No, I never attended the -- an SDS meeting. Yes, I had seen documents, I had listened to people talking to me. Yes, from those events the conclusion was inescapable, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you refer us to a particular SDS document which made you draw this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say an SDS document. Document, one of the strangest one, was Pasic's own written document which you, Dr. Karadzic, has referred to the Court - today, I forget which paragraph - and signed as crisis committee. That document came at the end of many many meetings where despite his own admission to me, he writes for official purposes something I know he didn't agree with, that is the voluntary nature of the evacuation. Just to name one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to it then. Dr. Kirudja, do you know that such things did not happen in the following municipalities: Bosanska Dubica, Gradiska, Srbac, Prnjavor, Sipovo, and others and a number of Muslim witnesses said so. Do you know of the reasons why it did not occur in these municipalities if, indeed, these were central instructions? In other words, if you are correct, why was it not implemented across the board starting with the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That was a hugely compound question, Dr. Karadzic, and I anticipate that if it stays in that form, Dr. Kirudja will be under an obligation to give a hugely compound answer. Do you want to try and define it rather better.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd be happy to. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, did you know that -- or do you agree that the crisis in Bosanski Novi occurred two or two and a half months later once the clashes had erupted all around that particular municipality?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that none of it happened in some other municipalities, too, where Muslims remained living together with the Serbs? It was actually the case in many municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cannot authenticate that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can you then confirm that you are unaware of any municipalities where the situation was not such?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Dr. Karadzic, the narrative talks of one particular meeting where my office was full of Bosnian officials from Sanski Most, from Bosanska Krupa, from Bosanski Novi, from Prijedor, from others. They brought me numbers, names, and lists. One of the most memorable one again is in the narrative, is a computer-printed list of the people they wanted out, numbering 7.782 from name number 1. So I don't support the point being made that we didn't hear it from anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Dr. Kirudja, please answer this question only: Do you know or did you know then that in Bosanska Krajina there were municipalities in which Muslims and Serbs lived together where nothing happened? Yes or no? Did you know that there was a number of such municipalities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't give you a yes or no because of the use of the word "Bosanska Krajina". Bosanska Krajina is a name encompassing those same, the opstinas that I named. There are five of them from Cazin, Bosanska most -- Sanski Most, and other, and Krupa, so when you rephrase them with this a collective name, the answer remains the way I answered earlier, we were hearing same things from those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way, Dr. Kirudja, were you aware of the existence of a demi-state formation called the Autonomous Region of the Krajina containing some 20 odd municipalities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in an entirely different context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the municipalities you enumerated save for Cazin were part of the ARK?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know every detail about it and, as I said, not wanting to prolong my answers, it was an entirely different context, I came to learn on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, it has to do with what you state in paragraph 79. You imply that there was a plan on a higher level, as well as a policy and instruction. I'm asking you, therefore, this: Do you know -- are you familiar with the structure of the RS at the time? Did you know of the existence of the ARK comprising some 20 municipalities and that many municipalities did not have this particular problem?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to return the answer on paragraph 79 to the context in which it was given. Your Honour, you note it was a session with the Judges on the Bench and the question was coming from one of the Judges, El Mahdi, it was a simple question whether I thought, he wanted to know, the SDS was playing a part in the events that I was telling them, and the answer speaks for itself, it begins with people come in, they would identify themselves, who they were, and then they will say what they wanted. And the rest I don't want to repeat the answer. That's the context in which the answer was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Hence you concluded that the inescapable conclusion was that they acted under instruction and policy from a higher body, a higher instance; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least from somebody else, not themselves, because they will come over and over again on the same matter. They will receive the same answer from me that we can't do this. They will ask who the superiors were. We will tell them, you can go all the way to the Secretary-General and you will not hear a different answer to the question whether you can force people to move away from their homes. Having gone that -- over and over again, the conclusion was these people were being -- on a policy to do something they themselves may not want to pursue personally that long and in the way they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, let us be precise, please. What is -- or what was this centre which in your conclusion led this policy or put it in place?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer contains the answer to Dr. Karadzic. I said somebody, not that somebody I knew. It was your acting under a force driven by something else. Doesn't mean that I knew who that somebody else was, and I don't at this moment say that I do know that. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the fact that we are discussing the context of the SDS, did you know that in April at the very beginning of the war on the prime minister's request, the SDS froze its activities until February 1993? Did you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the eastern part of Republika Srpska as well as Pale and Srpsko Sarajevo could not communicate with the western part in Banja Luka, Bosanski Novi and adjacent municipalities by phone, all the way until September 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. For example, the corridor was closed until the 1st of July, 1992, and it only became safe in September, and telephone communication was up and running in September as well, and when I say that, I mean communication between the eastern and western parts of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter 6688. There should be a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have the translation. We can just keep the translation there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on this, on the 18th of June, 1992, the Municipal Assembly -- so, the Municipal Assembly already met and the Crisis Staff is its organ, an organ of the regular authorities. Look at what it says here, paragraph 2: [As read] "with regard to the Muslim population of the Bosanski Novi municipality, the following positions of the SDS Municipal Board have been adopted: "First, that citizens of Muslim ethnicity may voluntarily leave the Bosanski Novi municipality in an organised and civilised manner. "Secondly, that any activities directed at forceful expulsion were strictly banned." And so on and so forth. And ultimately: "4, the Bosanski Novi public security station and military police command have been instructed to establish public law and order in Bosanski Novi and ensure the security of its inhabitants." Does paragraph 4 imply that public law and order have not been established yet and that the security of the citizens had not been ensured as yet?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing I note, Your Honour, on this memo, the date. The date is June 1992. The beginning of this discussion with Mayor Pasic began much earlier in May. The letter that warned, we just went through that letter, the letter that warned Mr. Pasic that what was being done could be considered a crime against humanity, I forget its date. Can I have that date, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The letter -- 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 20th of June, 1992. And this letter on the monitor is June what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 18th of June. Two days before your letter.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days before. We had already gone through this. We had notified many of our -- the people we spoke to. This was not something that was going to find favour inside the international community. And each time we did this and the narrative shows, they would soften with statements like: "We'll do the right thing." "We are mayor for all people." And this letter coming towards that end, which I had never seen before, I'm seeing it for the first time, reflects moving events from the time when this matter came up. That's how I -- my impression of it. Why? Because some of the things being said there were never said to us at the time when we met Mr. Pasic, the author of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kirudja. That will do as far as I'm concerned, but I'm asking about these conclusions that you drew without us giving you a full picture. Look at this, Dr. Kirudja, this is the 18th of June, this is a conclusion, it's not a letter, it's a conclusion. It's a binding conclusion of a state authority from a session that was held on the 16th of June. So there was no initiative that was launched from elsewhere. The Serb Democratic Party discussed this and this was ultimately adopted by the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, let me ask you, in paragraph 79 you say, "the milicija as they call it." Do you mean when you say "milicija," do you mean "militia" as the meaning is elsewhere in the world? But do you know that in our country, the regular police used to be called "milicija," "militia"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Dr. Karadzic, paragraph 79 has a reference to "milicija"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. [In English] "And since they identify themselves as the SDS or members of the militia or what they called ..."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you. Thank you, Dr. Karadzic. Yes, I understand that "milicija" in the context you explained referred to the regular police. This was a transcription of something I said live so the spelling not necessarily different from the pronunciation, as you can see, it's a transcript of something, not a document. Something I said live.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we do agree that you did not mean a party militia of the SDS? You meant the regular police force, the state police force that was called "milicija"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? This document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Let that be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1916, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there is a reference here to this civilised and organised manner of -- of having the population move out, and may I remind you that the same wording is contained in the agreement of the 22nd of May, that made it binding on all three of us, all three parties to act in that way?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I note what the document says is what you say, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have a look at 65 ter 6705.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned -- or actually in that UNHCR document there is a reference to the Red Cross. So let us see now a document of the Bosanski Novi municipality Red Cross dated the 7th of June, 1992. Yes, please take a look at this. This is a piece of information and it describes what was happening in Bosanski Novi where military operations were underway against Muslim extremists. There is a large concentration of Muslim people in Blagaj, their accommodation in Blagaj is temporary because the representatives of the displaced Muslims have asked for voluntary resettlement in Croatia. And then further on that's what that paragraph says. Then a bit further down, it says: [As read] "Also, operations are underway to cleanse the area around Blagaj of Muslim extremists who are hiding in the surrounding woods. Due to these operations there is a real danger of some groups getting out of the command and control mechanism and threatening the safety of people in Blagaj. It is proposed that the operation of volunteer resettlement to Banja Luka should continue, using their own means of transport or transport organised by the Crisis Staff." Further on, it says that one group -- actually, it says, "It is necessary that a convoy be set up by no later than" et cetera et cetera, and be escorted to Banja Luka by the military and police. Evacuation of the population from Bosanski Novi, Republika Srpska, to Banja Luka in Republika Srpska, would you call that ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it's a long, long statement and I'm wondering the "it" in the last bit of your statement, would you call that, that referring to what, ethnic cleansing, because it's a wrong statement. What do I attribute "that" to be in reference to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll deal with it slowly. Do you know that in our Law on Defence there is an obligation on the part of the authorities to evacuate civilians from combat areas into an area where there is no combat? Regardless of whether the population wanted to be evacuated or not, they have to be evacuated just like in America when there's a hurricane coming. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I wouldn't know what your law says about that specific issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let us move on to this now: If the population is asked to move for the sake of their own safety from one Serbian municipality into another Serbian municipality, is that ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be self-evident if they are being moved for safety from one part of Serbian-controlled areas to another. I guess it would be self-evident and would need no defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You would not call that ethnic cleansing; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not if people are being moved from, say, a natural disaster to a safer area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you consider war to be a natural disaster?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that our law states that it is compulsory for civilians to be evacuated from war zones, would you accept that that is the duty of the authorities to act accordingly even if it is an unnatural disaster?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends where you are moving them. If you cross international borders, your law wouldn't be applicable outside your jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in this case in Republika Srpska if they are being moved from one municipality to another is that ethnic cleansing or is that in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a circular question, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted. This document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1917, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly have a look at P2737.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Bosanska Krupa as well, right, and you also had some refugees from Bosanska Krupa; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did refer to them being notified of refugees coming from Bosanska Krupa, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please focus on this order. The president of the War Presidency of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. Let me ask you something, Mr. Kirudja, do you know in this case of Bosanska Krupa when one says Serb municipality, do you know what that means? Or should I help you? Do you know that that's the proposal of the Serb side, for these big municipalities to have two or three municipalities, and that the Serb Municipality of Bosanska Krupa only means the Serb part of that municipality?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the document you are displaying, Dr. Karadzic, or in general?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, Dr. Kirudja, if one says Serb municipality, did you know that this meant within the same municipality what was envisaged was that there should also be a Muslim municipality and a Croatian municipality or a Muslim and Croatian municipality? Did you know that this prefix "Serb" only pertained to part of the municipality that had a majority Serb population?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on that except in the areas where I was in the UNPA, if you place that question under UNPA, the answer is no, it wouldn't mean that because that was the order that prevailed before people went to war, under municipality was a municipality wholesome, inclusive of all citizens who lived in that municipality. The distinction whether it was Serb or somebody else's was as a result of the fighting and part of the issue that brought us there, making that specific distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I agree about Croatia, or rather the Serb Krajina, but you are testifying about Bosnia, and now I'm asking you the following: I mean, I'm not attacking you for not knowing, but did you know what it means when it says the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa? Did you know that it did not pertain to all of Bosanska Krupa but only the Serb part of the municipality? The right bank of the Una river?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept your characterisation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at this, this is an order issued to the commanders of the 2nd, 4th and 5th Battalion of the 1st Podgrmec Brigade to evacuate the Muslim population in the territory of Budimlic Japra, Kamengrad and Fajtevci. Did you know that Budimlic Japra, Kamengrad and Fajtevci are parts of Sanski Most, that was also under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us please have a look at 65 ter 6733.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please take a look at this. This is the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Novi and the Crisis Staff is an organ of that Municipal Assembly, rather it replaces the Executive Board, and this is a report on the work of the Crisis Staff during this period of time. Please focus on the second paragraph. The second paragraph, it says: "Other important issues". At that moment it was not easy to give an answer to them, where is Alija Izetbegovic's policy leading us to, and the other side is armed with what kind of weapons, and what it says here is that it was agreed that our positions and policy have to be joint ones and that we should not allow for different streams to exist, hardline, softline, and that we have to deal with criminals of all kinds, especially arms smugglers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know about this analysis?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this, where it says in the beginning of May the 4th of May, 1992, concrete talks started with the SDA in relation to the security situation. Do you agree that for already a month there had been a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the 6th of April onwards? For all of one month there had been a war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas here in Bosanski Novi there was no war?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at this. Here it says what the SDS and the SDA talked about. And what was mostly discussed was the involvement of the SDA and the arming of the Muslim people. And they denied it. And that was not accepted. Then a bit further down, it says that a curfew was imposed from 2200 hours until 5.00 a.m. and all persons, armed persons and paramilitary formations were asked to hand over their weapons by the 11th of May at the latest. And a bit further down it says there was a problem of the functioning of the Executive Board because the president was on sick leave and so on and so forth. Then he resigned, whereas members and candidates of the SDA obstructed the work of that committee. Do you see that already then on the 4th of May, an order was being issued to disarm those who had been armed illegally?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already testified the narrative does already reflect the summary from the mayor, Pasic, up to what happened on the 11th of May, at least that dead-line. Yes, I had been informed of that. Not from this source that is displayed here, but from the testimony -- from the meeting that I did with mayor of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page and then the bottom of the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just thinking in -- so that Mr. Karadzic doesn't continually read out slabs of this document, perhaps we could rise early and the English translation could be given to Dr. Kirudja to review over the lunch break and then Mr. Karadzic could perhaps put some questions to Dr. Kirudja on it. And by the way, it's Exhibit P2632. And the previous document that was put to Dr. Kirudja, 65 ter number 6724 is Exhibit P2737.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure that would assist Dr. Kirudja. Would that assist you, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would be of assistance, thank you, but I wonder about something else because there are a great many documents that have to do with Dr. Kirudja's service and his superior, Mr. Thornberry, who most probably will not be testifying, although we have been notified that he would be testifying. Could we kindly ask Dr. Kirudja to look at a bundle of these documents just to confirm their authenticity and then we could deal with them through a bar table motion so that we wouldn't have to call up each and every one of them. Would that be feasible, although in this way we would take away Dr. Kirudja's lunch break, or can he look at it later and just say whether that's it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Kirudja, I don't want to deprive you of your lunch --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's okay with you, lunch is not such an important component of my life. But if others feel differently, of course I'm not the only one who will eat lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I mean, eating and reading at the same time is of course potentially possible, Dr. Karadzic's suggestion, subject to anything that the Prosecution might say seems to me to be an eminently sensible way of saving a large chunk of your time. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that authenticity is in issue in relation to the UNPROFOR documents, so I wonder what the utility of the exercise would be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I anticipated a degree of authenticity might have been in issue from the nature of Dr. Karadzic's suggestion. Dr. Karadzic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. Indeed. I resisted offering many documents from the civilian affairs department of the UN because I expected Mr. Thornberry to come as a witness, however, I see that he is no longer on the witness list and I lost this chance of having these documents exhibited earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, of course, there's huge difference between authenticity and agreeing the contents of the documents. One would anticipate, I don't speak for him, I'm speaking generally, that Dr. Kirudja is not going to deny the authenticity of the documents or disagree with the authenticity of the documents, nor if it's his document disagree with the contents. But if there is some utility in what you suggest and it is going to enable you not to have to put those documents to Dr. Kirudja during the course of his testimony, it may still be a worthwhile exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, in that case I would definitely prepare all those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, since the witness has acquiesced in this, I'm simply concerned about any effort to conflate issues here so that there's confusion about what has happened, as Ms. Sutherland noted, there hasn't been in the past, that I am aware of, dispute about the authenticity of UN documents. We don't anticipate such here. It doesn't change the protocol for bar table submissions or cross-examination. I'm really not sure what is being accomplished. But if there's, as the Court has noted, some aspect here that is being missed and that might be facilitated by the witness's review, of course we don't object. At the same time, I think it is a difficult task to be a witness. Everyone else is going to take a break. This witness should be permitted to at least, I guess, take a short break so that he can continue with the concentrated task of giving evidence when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Seems that Dr. Kirudja is made of stern stuff, from what he says, so if there is going to be -- I can't quite identify or focus on the utility myself at the moment but that may be a defect in my observations rather than anything else, but if it is going to save time in the long run, maybe it can be done. Our thanks to Dr. Kirudja for undertaking the task and we'll break now until 1.35.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I can suggest that some of it can be looked at by Dr. Kirudja in hard copy during the court session and maybe he can say yes, this is a document that reflects what I experienced or what the civilian affairs did. Maybe he can -- does not have to use his entire break for this exercise. I'm really embarrassed now for having suggested that he should use his free time to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I don't think your embarrassment is reflected in Dr. Kirudja's own feelings, so see how we get on. You give the documents to Dr. Kirudja or facilitate the giving of the documents to Dr. Kirudja that you think he is going to be useful for him to peruse over the lunch break and we will meet again at 1.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, I'm sorry we are starting a few minutes later than anticipated, but now we are on track and. Were you able to have any useful dealings with the witness in terms of what he was able to read over the lunch period?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. We perused the documents that we managed to print out. I believe that Dr. Kirudja is familiar with all of them and we will able to use them later. Maybe Dr. Kirudja can tell us whether he is satisfied with what he saw, in other words, that he saw what he needed to see in order to confirm the authenticity of the documents. In the meantime, I would like to have a document admitted. It is 23030. This is a UNHCR letter to Mr. Pasic. We already saw the document before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, that can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1918, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja. Thank you for your assistance over the lunch break. Are you able to assist with any comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure how you want to go over the documents. Yes, I have received the documents and there would be no difficulties for me to validate the authenticity, though some of them were written a long long time ago, the content will slowly come to me if they became relevant for discussion, but by looking at them it is not too difficult to authenticate their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll leave it in Dr. Karadzic's hands a to which of them he wants to produce with you, and which he doesn't. Thank you. Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up 65 ter 6732.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, I'm very sorry that you couldn't -- did not see all the documents issued by the authorities in Bosanski Novi. If you had been able to do that, I'm sure that you would realise that chaos reigned there, there was a state of civil war. As you said it yourself, war approached Bosanski Novi, there was war going on in many municipality -- many settlements in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Novi. You said that yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. One moment. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Dr. Kirudja could have answered the question, but I'd simply wanted to advise that 65 ter number 6732 is part of Defence exhibit D00470.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I do apologise for interrupting in between the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Karadzic for your comment about what I may have or may have not concluded had I seen of some of the documents that were internal to the officers of the Serbian Republic or Srpska Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I am not sure how that plays out in hindsight, looking at documents in hindsight, so I'll let his comments stand as it is, as a possibility that I may reach a different conclusion, although I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please pay attention to line 10 where it says 1500 hours. There is a description of the activity on the volunteer surrender of weapons with mixed result and it says that the military police reported that they had been attacked, and then on the 24th of May, the entire population from the villages in the valley of the Japra was accommodated in the central part of Blagaj Japra, and then it says that on the 2nd of June, forces of the municipal staff of Bosanski Novi Territorial Defence and the military police, without the knowledge of the Bosanski Novi public security station and without consultation with it, brought in citizens who were not ethnically Serbian to the Mlakve stadium. It is also stated here that ac cording to their information, the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence carried out this action in order to stop uncontrolled groups and individuals who, apart from retaliating against the population, were committing acts of wanton destruction against all buildings. Furthermore, it says on the following page that that centre was disbanded on the 5th of June which means three days after it was set up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And everybody went home, save for 17 persons who were kept on the premises of the military police. It also says here that the citizens had at their disposal both the sports and the social facilities of the football club and were regularly provided with food and water. Further on there is a reference -- just a moment, bear with me. On the 24th of May, again around 4.000 inhabitants, yes, it is here, but I believe that the translation is really bad. On the 24th of May, around 4.000 inhabitants left their homes and became refugees. They went to the central part of the village of Blagaj and then, on the 9th of June, it was agreed that they would go to the railway station, they would board 22 railway carriages and they would be transported in the direction of Doboj. Did you know that the first time they refused to go to Doboj and then the second time accepted to go to Doboj? The difference between the two events was 17 days. First they refused to be taken to Doboj, they returned to their homes, and then 17 days later, they agreed to be transported to Doboj.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, is your question to me to confirm that they did what you said they did?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. I just wanted to know whether you knew that a train was brought in, that they were offered to be taken to Doboj but they refused to board the train, they went home because they wanted to go to Croatia. Did you know that the first time around they refused to be transported to Banja Luka because they wanted to be taken to Croatia. They spent 17 days at home before they eventually decided that they would agree to be transported to Doboj.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that particular detail that Dr. Karadzic has described to the Court, but I would like to add one clarification. About that same period he is talking about, those very people were also engaging us with a different story. The first time they formed an SOS in the field, observed by military observers, Danish, and from the war, and that drew our attention and from there we were receiving their story. That's not to say I know or don't know what Dr. Karadzic is saying. I want Dr. Karadzic to be aware about that time we were also looking and we were receiving a different story from those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that. I only want to know whether you knew that they were in a position to refuse, that they indeed refused to travel in the depth of the Republika Srpska because they wanted to go to Croatia. If you didn't know that, I would find that fact important as well. You didn't know that, did you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know what they were refusing to do. They said to us they were refusing to do different things than the one you -- it may be true they were refusing what you are saying, but they said they were refusing to do other things too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony so far you have confirmed that the causes of the migration of the population were civil war and chaos that reigned supreme in the area; is that correct? You also stated that the civilian population under the war were suffering and continued to suffer due to the large number of cases despite a cease-fire. You said that, for example, in the Brdjanin case on the 10th of February -- or rather, 2003 on page 14580. I'm going to read in English, just a little bit. You explained at the time that a larger number of displaced people were a result of war primarily in Croatia and subsequently a result of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that there were a lot of Serbs who were refugees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the last statement that you have made is correct, if you characterise my testimony as implying what is stated in the last statement, but it is not correct at the beginning of your statement that my testimony confirmed the causes of migration of the population were civil war and chaos that reigned supreme in the area. It's not a proper characterisation of my testimony. My testimony was I wanted to know the causes of why they were moving and I was asking what the causes were. I was not naming the causes. I asked where is the pressure coming from, why do they want to move. That's a characterisation of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you not say in the Brdjanin case on page 14584 that if somebody found themselves embroiled in a conflict they would want to move somewhere, for example, to Austria or Germany where their family resided or anywhere else where there was no conflict and that would not be an unusual thing to experience, didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need an exact reference for where I said that. I have a feeling that there is something missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, I anticipate you were rising for just that point. Do you have an exact reference, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page numbers 14584 in the Brdjanin case and it was recorded on the 10th of February, 2003, or actually, on the 13th of February. In e-court, it is 6522681.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is a reference to a United Nations report from 1991 where it is stated that that was not an unusual thing to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Karadzic isn't going to bring the page up in e-court, Dr. Kirudja's taken to a document in cross-examination and then his answer is "that is what the report states." That's the only answer that he gives on page 14584.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that's going to assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what made me feel that there was something missing in the earlier characterisation of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, do you agree with me that you could find that in the United Nations report and that your answer was to the following effect, that if there is a war going on and if somebody finds themselves in the midst of the situation that it wouldn't be unusual for that person to want to go to Germany or Austria where their families reside, for example, or to another area where there was no war or conflict?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my testimony appears as you have put it in those very words, I would be surprised to include Germany or Austria if I was speaking in generalities, that is it human to try to escape from danger. That's all it says, if you wanted a brief short of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, again it's a Defence question which puts a proposition and then the answer is as it -- Dr. Kirudja asks the question: "You mean as a general question?" And then the answer is yes. And then Dr. Kirudja's answer, he said: "No, it wouldn't be." So I think that Mr. Karadzic needs to actually bring the pages up on the screen if he is going to put questions -- prior transcript to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, you can't ascribe a question to the witness unless he adopts the whole of the question in his answer. It's patently unfair to do that and doesn't assist.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we will leave this topic aside for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Muslim representatives told you that they wanted to go to third countries for various reasons because of fighting, for economic reasons, because of some uncontrolled individuals that the Serbian authorities tried to put under their control but failed in that attempt; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct that Muslim representatives told me what follows in that sentence. I have gone to painful length to mention time and time again, Muslims interests were being relayed to me by Serbs, not Muslims themselves saying to me this is what we want to do, with the exception of the refugees who would find they have been able to escape and before we take them to safety we would ask what was going on and where do you want to go. With that clarification, some of them will say, we want to go somewhere in Europe or some other named places in Europe. Not a Muslim representative talking about we want to go to Germany or Austria. I want that clarification made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you that they wanted to leave for economic hardships because they were poor? Did they also say to you that they were afraid of retaliation for every Serb who died in the front line? Did they say that up to that time the Serbian authorities managed to prevent any such attempts of retaliation and that they said that their movement should not be considered ethnic cleansing but rather that it should be put in the context of threats on their life?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Karadzic. I think you are talking about a very specific report of the narrative where a Muslim representative somewhere in Kostajnica met with me and my colleagues. He was an engineer by profession, and he had been selected by the Serbs and he was talking very deferentially about the Serbs beginning his statement with, "I've been authorised to say this ...," and I took note of that. And in that case what Dr. Karadzic is saying is correct, he would say, we need to leave because of economic reasons. We need not to be here if there is a fighting and as long as Serbs are killed we fear there will be repercussions. If that's what Dr. Karadzic is talking about, yes, it does appear in my testimony, but within the context I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said this in paragraph 105 of your statement, you mention engineer Saflic and then in paragraph 109 you say that a certain Muslim representative then added that they fear reprisals each time Serbs are killed at the confrontation line. And it also says that, so far, the Serbian authorities have managed to prevent such reprisals. Did you hear that from that same Muslim or from some other Muslim?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Karadzic, I couldn't have remembered the paragraphs where this story was. Yes, that's in the context which that story was told, and no, I, at this moment, wouldn't be able to say it was the only person who said that in the entire engagement that I had. If there was somebody else who may have said it elsewhere in a different context, that may also be entirely possible. But I want to repeat, there were people who had been brought by Serbian people in authority and you could see they were trying very much to be correct, to be deferential, and to say the right things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you would say that that was an artificial situation and you did not trust such Muslims, you didn't believe their stories, did you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Dr. Karadzic. When people are frightened, there is nothing artificial about it. I believed what they were saying, but it wouldn't amount to the wishes of general Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in paragraph 113, for example, you say that Islamcevic told you that he was authorised to request that UNPROFOR escort the convoy. You say this: [In English] [As read] "He claimed that those requesting evacuation Did not want to go from one part of BiH to another. That they had guarantees from relatives to support them elsewhere, that the Serbian authorities were treating them fairly and that they wanted to ensure that no one was taken from the convoy until they reached Karlovac."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my testimony and I'm saying exactly that. But I knew I had received this kind of request whether they were in the company of Serbs or they were alone, as long as they are in the territory controlled by the Serbs, they would not breathe a sigh of relief until they get out, and they measured their words, what they said. They didn't know who was listening and who would say anything. So we took what they were saying, and you can see this is my testimony, I cannot say this is somebody else's. It's my testimony. This is what happened, but I'm characterising it, what it meant to us. Often we would keep them under civil police guards until they got out. There was a reason for that, they were fearful for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Dr. Kirudja, the way you understood things, that was a very subjective thing and it depended on your willingness to believe one thing or the other. For example, people believe in God only if they want to believe in God. If you want to believe that that was the case, then you believed it. But I'm putting it to you that here somebody told you that they didn't want to be moved to a different part of Bosnia but that they had guarantees from their families to join them somewhere else. Are you denying that? Wouldn't this mean that they really wanted and requested to go somewhere outside of Bosnia, and you have just told us that they didn't ask you to be transferred abroad?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have misunderstood me, Dr. Karadzic. I didn't say any of that. I said that I believe that's what they wanted, and if they wanted a safe passage, we would provide it. It's not that they didn't say wanted to go where they wanted to go. What I'm telling the Court is that Dr. Karadzic also is saying that was the general wish of the Muslims and that's my only point of difference with what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Dr. Kirudja, I have to make a distinction between your subjective impression and irrefutable facts. This is something that is mandatory in a criminal proceedings. I'm putting it to you that when people left Bosnia they didn't want to be repatriated, and that with that goal in mind, they would say anything, they would say that there were no conditions in place for their repatriation. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, I've said all I'm going to say on that point and Mr. Karadzic's point is noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, again, you are asking the witness to, as it were, speculate about what people may or may not have had as a genuine agenda as opposed to what they said to him. All the witness can tell the Court is what people said to him at the time. And I think this topic really is exhausted now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I've been encouraged by the witness himself because he, himself, speculates about Muslim intentions, so if he can speculate on that, I suppose that he can speculate on other things as well. But let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Kirudja, that there's not a single place in Bosnia where a certain number of Muslims did not stay living peacefully until the very end of the war?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you can tell us whether you know or whether you don't know. Are you saying that you don't know that in Republika Srpska in every single place a certain significant number of Muslims stayed because they didn't want to go anywhere? I'm not saying that that was indeed the case, I'm just asking you whether you knew that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I am sorry, Dr. Karadzic, that's a -- a very bizarre question. It's complete non sequitur. It's an unanswerable question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Kirudja, that in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina no single Serbian place remained standing, whereas in Republika Srpska there are a lot of Muslim and Croatian villages that nobody touched?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same answer. I will never be able to say that. No single place, I will never be able to utter that statement as a statement of truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you, Mr. Kirudja, that that is the truth, but I would like to hear it from you as a person who has a standpoint, who had a view, who wrote reports. I would like to know whether you knew that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The witness has already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The witness has already answered that question, Dr. Karadzic, but you've got to be very cautious. Putting a statement as if it was an established fact and then asking the witness if he knew it is not a true question. First of all, it assumes that the leading part of the question is in fact factually true, and secondly, if the witness denies it, that's the end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent, Your Excellency, but in my layperson's understanding of the law, I will be able to prove that many villages remained intact, for example, Srbac, Sipovo, and we heard that from Muslim witnesses here. I have time, I want to prove whether there's any grounds for Mr. Kirudja's conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, as I understand it is not making conclusions. He is saying he can't answer, he can't confirm something which he doesn't know to be the case. If you are going to, in due course, adduce evidence as opposed to comment that a certain matter is true, then that's a different -- completely different matter, but that's not the object of the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Excellency, I would like to establish how Dr. Kirudja formed his opinions. Was it based on his overall knowledge of the situation, thorough knowledge of the situation, or partial knowledge of the situation. Let me ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know, Dr. Kirudja, that Catholic and Muslim officials still live in the Republika Srpska whereas Orthodox church officials cannot be found anywhere in the Federation? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again I will not be able to answer that and let me be very specific, I need to be in every place to answer that question. I have never been in every place. So it wouldn't be possible to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, do you know that we initiated and always accepted other people's initiatives for all the sides to commit themselves to allow the return of all refugees once the final peace accord was signed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first time I'm hearing from you that this was so. I didn't know before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that such an obligation was not up to the municipal authorities, but rather to the central authorities of Republika Srpska who actually negotiated both with the international community and with the other two parties?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know what was transpiring between the municipal authorities and the central authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. I do not mean negotiations between the municipal and central authorities, but would you agree me that the right of return was something that was negotiated at the level of the central government of all three parties and not at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 111, you say that in Topusko you met -- you and UNHCR met with a delegation of Serbs and Muslims from Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa and Prijedor. Would you please take a look at that paragraph. And there you also say that you also met with Vlado Vrkes and Dragan Majkic, police chief of Sanski Most, with Mr. Besim Islamcevic, representatives of Muslims and Croats, who wanted to leave Sanski Most. Mr. Esad Hasanovic, who was also representative, or rather, he was in Sanski Most where he found himself after he left Bosanska Krupa; is that correct? Would you agree this Hasanovic person fled from Bosanska Krupa to Sanski Most which was in Republika Srpska, in fact?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't have known that specific detail about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [In English] [As read] "Mr. Esad Hasanovic, the Sanski Most-based representative of Muslims and Croats willing to leave Bosanska Krupa." [Interpretation] Is that correct, so he was from Bosanska Krupa and they wanted to leave Bosanska Krupa but he was actually based in Sanski Most, he was in a Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is paragraph 111 of your statement and then in paragraph 112 you say that the delegation tried to convince the United Nations to change its policy against mass evacuations associated with ethnic cleansing and to assist in the organisation of another convoy through Sector North that would serve to evacuate 11.000 mostly Muslim applicants for evacuation from Sanski Most, and 8.000 from Prijedor. So here we have a mixed delegation, Muslims, representatives, authorised representatives, together with Serb. We have the two sides telling you that; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's what I'm reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in paragraph 116, Vrkes confirms before these Muslims that 25.000 persons, probably Muslim, had come from Bosanska Krupa and were now living in Sanski Most, and then he says: [In English] "Only Sanski Most is looking after all three nationalities ..." And he said that in the presence of the Muslim representatives; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you confirm in the same paragraph that before the arrival of the Muslim population from Bosanska Krupa, Sanski Most had a population of 50 per cent of Serbs, 50 per cent of Muslims, and that once the refugees -- Muslim refugees arrived, that ratio, that balance had changed, and then he said that they never mentioned and felt that they were in any way, these Muslims and Croats, that they in any way posed danger to the Serbs, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one correction, I'm not the one who confirmed the ratio of Muslims to Serbs. It's Mr. Vrkes who is reporting the ratios. I'm not confirming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, this is something that was reported to you by a mixed delegation, both to you and the UNHCR, on the 18th of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now briefly take a look at 1D4828, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, by any chance, what the meaning of Merhamet is, or rather, do you know that Merhamet is a Muslim charity?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4828. 1D4828. Maybe there was an error of some sort. My apologies, 4829.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let me tell you this: Merhamet is a Muslim humanitarian organisation that was active in Republika Srpska throughout this period providing aid to Muslims, civilians, or prisoners of war and they even engaged some of its members in spying, not all of them, of course, but throughout this period, they were allowed to remain there and be active just as was the case with Caritas, a Catholic charitable organisation. So do you know throughout this period they were allowed to operate in Republika Srpska unfettered?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, please take a look at this report. It is a report on the activities of Merhamet in Novi Grad and Bosanski Novi. I don't know if we have a translation but I will read this out to you: [As read] "According to our records, the Muslim humanitarian organisation has so far provided for 2.880 citizens humanitarian aid and it could be broken down as follows: 2.300 Muslims were helped, as well as 500 individuals from mixed marriages, and individuals who needed social assistance." So we can see from this that throughout the war Merhamet was able to provide aid, humanitarian aid, to citizens in Novi Grad, and do you understand now that in 1994 there were 2.300 Muslims still living in this town.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we take a look at the date, then, at the top. Do you know that only villagers from those villages where there was fighting moved out, whereas in Novi Grad, the people remained, they stayed put?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you agree that this is a report that was issued on the 25th of May, 1994? Can you take a look, please.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at it and it has the date you mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Kirudja hasn't confirmed anything in the document except for the confirming the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's difficult to see how this document is going to assist in respect of this witness, Dr. Karadzic. As Ms. Sutherland said, he has not confirmed anything. The date is self-evident. I can't see at the moment how it can be usefully or properly admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Excellency, but let me read out the paragraph that can barely be made out at the end. It says: [As read] "From a drugstore where there also individuals of Serb nationality, over 5.000 different medications were issued at the request of the Merhamet. Of 11th May, 1994, the ministry of national Defence of Stari Grad approved the work obligation for 16 Muslims, five of whom were men, whereas four were medical workers at the drugstore and doctors of Merhamet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the second part of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: At the moment, I don't see the utility of that. Is that going to form part of the question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was my question, whether the witness who took a position here, which was not in favour of Serbs, was he aware of the whole picture? Was he familiar with the full situation in the municipality next to the municipality of which he was testifying or on which he was testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document is dated May 1994. What relevance has it got to Dr. Kirudja's evidence about the events that he was testifying to in Bosanski Novi in 1992 and all the hostages in 1995 which is a separate issue, but I see no relevance to Dr. Kirudja's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's opaque at the moment. Dr. Kirudja, can you -- we've had the whole of this document before you now, in effect. Does any part of this document -- are you able to confirm the accuracy of any part of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document is totally unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: There you have it, Dr. Karadzic. A document to be admitted must have some utility as well the other tests, at the moment as far as this witness is concerned with respect to the term, there is no utility.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For your information, and I'm not insisting on it, I would just like to remind you that in the document Dr. Kirudja confirmed early on, that's 23030, mention was made of Merhamet and contact was sought with Merhamet and that's where I found the link. Now, as for my understanding for the basis on which Dr. Kirudja drew his conclusions, I'm trying to establish whether his conclusions were based on the knowledge of the full truth. But we will try to do that through some other document. Could we now see D1680.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Sorry, I just wanted to point out while I notice it, on lines 13 and 14 of this part of the transcript, what I actually said is there is no utility, not that there is utility, but that can be corrected, and I'm sorry I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that's what it says, there is no utility. At least that's what it says in LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It may be my screen is just not showing that, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at this document. We see that this is a session of the Executive Committee of the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly held on the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]Now, can we just scroll down this document or rather can we show page 4. In English that may be page 3. Kalcun? Kalacun? [In English] [As read] "I would like to ask the chairman of the Executive Committee to inform us of the general position of the Krajina R government on the exodus from the Serbian state."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here the president of the municipality, Rasula, says there is no general position, there are no instructions, and nobody can be forced to go into exile. The basic principle is that citizens should decide on their own where they want to live, and so on and so forth. [In English] [As read] "If they want to leave, they should be allowed to leave with certain supervision and protection. Those who wish to remain in the municipality will be allowed to stay only if they have not participated in any underhand activities. Those who wish to leave, they have to cover the costs of their journey, because we have no resources for this." [Interpretation] Did you know and do you agree that here the president of the municipality is stating that there are no instructions and that the basic rule is that citizens should decide on their own?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I note what you are saying, Dr. Karadzic, but I do not reconcile it with what they said to me in my office, and it's around paragraph 112 of my testimony narrative, that 600 people wanted to leave Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But would you take a look at the entire paragraph where you say: [In English] [As read] "The delegation, this is the mixed delegation, Serbs and the Muslims and the representative of Croats, the delegation intended to convince the UN to change its policy against mass evacuation associated with ethnic cleansing and to assist in the organisation of another convoy ...," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] I would like to remind you, Dr. Kirudja, that under our law there is a duty that -- or obligation that civilians should be moved out of combat areas, whether they wish to or not. And here they are requested to do so. So is it correct, is this what they said to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, again a conflicting point being made. They must leave by our law, they must not be pushed to leave because every citizen have the right to decide. That's what I'm hearing on one hand, what I'm hearing now on the other. My testimony was not those arguments, it's simply 600 people want to leave. It's a straightforward testimony, not a reasoned one. It's a statement of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, perhaps I was imprecise. What I'm trying to say is that in spite of this legal obligation, they are appealing to you and otherwise the authorities had the obligation to move the population, the civilians from combat areas. Here they are not applying, not abiding by that rule, they are appealing to you, this mixed delegation, they are appealing to you to help with their evacuation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They are asking. And they are receiving an answer also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now see what you have to say about the football stadium. Do you accept what I'm going to say now that civilians came to the football stadium where they were kept for two and a half days. On the third day, most of them were let -- allowed to go home except 120 of them who joined our army and 17 who were kept, who were detained by the military police for security reasons?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, for clarification, this testimony has two football fields and the people gathered, one very early in Karlovac, 1.600, and another in a football field in Bosanski Novi. For my clarification, is it football field in Bosanski Novi or in Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that in Karlovac, which is in Croatia, far the river or from the border, Croats accommodated 1.600 Muslims who were on their way back to Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they held them there in the football field due to the numbers. If that's what is called accommodation, I want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what I was referring to was the football stadium in Bosanski Novi where civilians from the Japra river valley were put up, so that's a different stadium and that's what you are referring to in paragraph 95 where you say that a Danish man from the Danish patrol saw, through his binoculars, the stadium in Bosanski Novi and he was able to report on the events there; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If paragraph 56 you say that 350 displaced person came from Kostajnica, or rather, that a Danish company in Kostajnica reported that 350 persons were displaced and gathered in a football field in Bosanski Novi. And then on the 8th of June, you report to Mr. Thornberry in a memo, which summarised the events between the 26th of May and 8th of June and you say: [In English] [As read] "... and placed those events within the context of the UN mandates, specifically I explained that according to CIVPOL sources in the war, the persons originally held in the stadium were all males. The women later seen were probably bringing food and other necessities to them." [Interpretation] So you prepared this report based on reports that were submitted to you by others; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gathering of the report was made by the Danish, but once they have gathered it, they would stop at that action, so it's forwarded to me. It's not gathered for themselves. It's gathered and forwarded to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 71, you say: [In English] [As read] "The report states that the persons being held in the football stadium reportedly waved white flags and flashed SOS to attract attention. The following day I transmitted this information again in a memorandum with a letter attached." [Interpretation] And a little lower down: [In English] "As noted in my report, this paragraph was designed to reinforce a message that had repeatedly been orally conveyed to him and his colleagues in Dvor by UNHCR and by me."
