[Interpretation] So this is a reference to Mr. Pasic. Now, first let me ask you this: Do you believe that these villagers actually knew how to signal SOS and wave the white flags -- with white flags? And could you explain perhaps, what kind of signalling that was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the one things soldiers do very well is read signals when they are trained to do that. They are watching in a tower and they see that and it's not a military situation. So the first thing is to say we are looking at this, we are seeing SOS, we don't know what it means and they are waving. That's the most I can say about that. And I'm saying it as a fact, not whether they knew how to do it, who was doing it, but it was being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is what you were told and you don't have any other information other than what was relayed to you? In other words, someone told you that they could see someone signalling with white flags, signalling an SOS?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, that someone is someone on duty charged with the responsibility to do something. It's not some busybody just observing for curiosity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you notified that a white flag placed on a house or on someone's arm means that the person in question was not a fighter and that the building in question was not involved in fighting in any case? This was done so that no fire would be opened on it. It was in daily use. In other words, the white flag or cloth meant: Do not shoot at me or at the house.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I note that in paragraph 71 it actually says the words flashing SOS, "waved white flags and flashed SOS," and the inference seems to me from there that the waving of the white flags and the flashing of the SOS were two separate acts and flashing strongly suggests a light source, which would mean that the SOS was being transmitted in Morse code, at least that's the inference I would draw, and I suspect many others would too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you merely conveyed this report, did you not? This was not your conclusion, you were merely conveying information; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, this paragraph has a lot to do with a lot of things that cannot be captured with the word "merely." It was a huge dispute going on whether or not at my headquarters they had been given this information on time. And they were claiming that I should have informed them earlier. This is what this paragraph is talking about, why didn't we know earlier than you told us. That's what this paragraph is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at something. You discuss this stadium in Bosanski Novi. Did you know that it was in the southern part of town at an altitude of 121 metres?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Dr. Karadzic, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Danish Battalion was in Dvor. Their observation post was at 126 metres above sea level. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know because I didn't query them about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know then that the observation bases of the UN were in Divusa which is 12 kilometres away from the stadium in Kostajnica which is 25 kilometres away, and in Dvor, and I would like to ask you how far the observation station in Dvor was from the stadium?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Dr. Karadzic, I can't tell you that. All I can tell you that the observation was not done from Kostajnica. It was done from Dvor on the river side. Not quite close to the river, but just about a few metres.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D4827.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Brdjanin case you testified that they observed it from their observation tower across the river, and that they used binoculars. Do you agree that this is Dvor on one end towards the top and down below we have the stadium at Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks vaguely correct. I've never looked at it from this angle before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree then that the location of the observation tower is 5.18 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because I can't tell just looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Google Earth automatically calculates distances and that is infallible, it automatically calculates any distance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that's asking the witness to agree with something which, unless he is an expert on Google Earth, I doubt that he can automatically agree. The point you are making is this: That if these distances marked on the aerial photograph are correct, 1.6 and 5.18 kilometres respectively, you are trying to make the point that it would be difficult, if not impossible, for the Danish soldiers to see what they said they saw, is that the object of the exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It goes both for the distance and vantage point because they were at an equal level basically, 121 and 126 metres above sea level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Are you in a position, Dr. Kirudja, to comment on that, or is that simply something outside your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only a simpler comment, Your Honour. I return to this evidence, it was not a contested evidence, the Danish were not being taken to task about what they saw or didn't see, and the Danes are pretty sophisticated military personnel, they were not asked what type of equipment you are using. Absent all of that, I wouldn't know what Dr. Karadzic's point amounts to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have a transcript page reference for that Brdjanin testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 12th of February, 2003. Page 14474 and 14475.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, did you know on which side the main seats were? On the western side we have the stands reaching up to 25 metres. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to deal next with the issue of statements you received from Muslim refugees. In paragraph 74 you say that you sent a report to UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb entitled "Humanitarian aid". [In English] [As read] "... which addressed the situation in Bosanski Novi and other places of detention in north-western Bosnia. In that report I said, we believe the football field detainees are only a tip of the iceberg involving the concerted action of local Serbian authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina trying to establish a Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina free of Muslims. In that process, the mayor, the milicija, the police, and the Territorial Defence forces of Bosanski Novi were acting in unison with their counterparts, not only in the UNPA (Dvor and Kostajnica), but also with (other Bosnian Serb authorities in) Bosanska Dubica, Banja Luka, Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc." [Interpretation] Then you go on to say: [In English] "The Serbs appear to be engaged in a determined process of forcefully disarming Muslims where they are a clearly a small encircled minority, such as in Bosanski Novi or besieging their city totally, such as in Bihac. Apparently the football field (in Bosanski Novi) is the holding ground where Muslim groups are detained while their houses are being searched, the men isolated and transported to concentration camps. The UNHCR representative and civil affairs have pieced together reports from Muslims who recently have taken refuge under UNPROFOR protection in Dvor and Kostajnica. There are reported concentration camps at the following locations:" [Interpretation] And then you enumerate them. We'll get to that. So you say specifically that you believe it was all happening as described in paragraph 79. Did you form that belief, as you say, based on what you were told by Muslim refugees or did you have any other proof?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have a date of this, this was a memorandum, the one that begins with we, that I released under my signature, and I don't have a date on it and it would be helpful if I knew the date because of what I'm going to say. We had gone through enormous reporting to the headquarters even as the pace of the people coming to where we were was picking up. That night when we wrote this thing, we were up almost 24 hours with a huge group of people, but we also didn't want them to leave before we debriefed them why they were leaving. As we were debriefing them, and this was not a small group of people, this information was repeated over and over again. Not by one, not by ten, we are talking about hundreds of people. Then we put together this document because at this moment I was distinctly aware that my headquarters was paying no attention to what I was saying, and then when the document got leaked, this document, the one you are looking at, by somebody I don't know, because I had copied it to both the UNHCR and the ICRC, it created at this moment so much brouhaha, there were about 30 reporters the next day in my office about this. At that moment, the entire matter gripped the Security Council and this document was an exhibit in there. So I wrote it in a very concise culminating to all the other reports that went before it -- this is an answer to the question where did the information come from. It was a culmination of all these reports triggered by a night of hundreds of people reporting the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to take a break now until 3.30. Ms. Sutherland, do you have any or are you likely to have any re-examination for Dr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a few minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Very well. We have a maximum period of time until 5.30 which gives an hour and a half and, Dr. Kirudja, I understand you have to fly tomorrow; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I appreciate your forbearance with it. There are many many things on hold since I came here last Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I thought so. There you have it, Dr. Karadzic. We have to finish your cross-examination of Dr. Kirudja and we've already extended it by an hour and a half from the original allotment and can you finish, please, by quarter past 5.00. We'll rise now until 3.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Before the break, I omitted to take into consideration the interpreters, which I should have done. What we are going to do is sit from now until 4.30, take a quarter of an hour break then resume sitting to 5.30. Dr. Karadzic, while it's on my mind, you asked if the court would not sit on the 21st of November, that's a possibility, but in order not to lose any sitting, instead we would sit on the afternoon of the 28th of November, which means that that week we'll be sitting each of the five days. If that's not going to conflict with any pre-made plans by the Defence, that can be put into operation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you saying that we would not be sitting on the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, we would not sit on the 21st, instead we would sit on the afternoon of the 28th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I hope, Mr. President, that was by way of clarifying Dr. Karadzic's request, meanwhile we have been attempting to determine the extent of any impact on witness scheduling based on the earlier assumption that we would still have four days of courtroom time on the week of the 21st. Now, I understand that the additional day lost on the 21st would be made up on the 28th, so we have to recalculate the effect of the loss of the 21st on witnesses including at least one of whom was fixed for a certain day on the week of the -- on the week of the 21st and others who have various travel arrangements that had been dependent upon the identified date. We are looking at that. We'd like to be accommodating if possible, but we have an obligation to consider the impact on the witnesses who have been advised on the basis of the previous schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Tieger. I'd assumed that that a was taken into account and I -- if that's just a misapprehension on my part then I'm sorry, you'll probably let us know as soon as practicable. Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we briefly look at 3842. Which is P3842.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document which was drafted by one of your associates, Raffone?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need the Serbian version, we can -- we don't need the Serbian version. Please bring back the English version. We don't need the Serbian version. On the 13th of July, 1992, and can we please have the following page on the screen. [In English] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this memorandum which was sent by Paolo Raffone, your associate or rather, your assistant?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the entire paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says here that -- that UNHCR crossed into Bosanski Novi and met representatives of Muslim population wanting and preparing to leave. [In English] [As read] "Despite all explanations their attitude he remained the same, that is, that their only possibility is to leave Bosnian Krajina for destinations in Croatia, Slovenia, and Western Europe."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I note that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were told that and this is not a Serbian source, it is Muslim representatives who informed UNHCR of what their intentions were and it seems that their intentions took them away from Bosnia and Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the break you told us that you had sent several reports to Zagreb to the staff there; however, those reports were not taken seriously. You also spoke about that in the Brdjanin case on the 10th of February, 2003. The transcript page number is 14488. Where you say that there were no reports or requests for the matter to be investigated, nobody paid attention to the memos that you sent them. Is all that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general idea is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on you said, and then you confirmed earlier today, that those reports had a large impact because they contained terms such as "concentration camps" and "unspeakable atrocities," and also that that should have provoked some sort of action but yet nobody paid any attention to them in the staff; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. It says up to that time nobody was paying attention. Up to that time. Second point, the word "concentration camp" is in quotes because it became a focus of attention. The language used by me introducing the memorandum itself wasn't as meritorious of attention as the key word "concentration camp," yet that is the word being used over and over again by the people running away from there, and the interpreters, like the one I'm listening to now, interpreted what they were saying as "concentration camps". That became such concern that the moment they paid attention to the memorandum, General Nambiar called me about it and his concern was whether that word was appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The only source of information that you had and the only grounds on which you based those terms and drafted those reports were interviews with those Muslims who had fled from Bosnia; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the only terms, but a critical part of it. I note you are using the word "only" source. I would replace that word as a critical part of that. It wasn't the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you make any attempts to check the words of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We made every conscious attempt that we could to cross-reference, to check information, being careful of the limited number of credible sources that could go into the issues that we were researching or reporting on. As long as we were able to find corroborative sources, we did so but we also did so on a point I made earlier to that, we were required to report these things as soon as possible, maximum within 24 hours. So we didn't have the luxury of doing comprehensive reports. We were reporting the information as it came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My first question, what other sources, can you tell us? Maybe we can verify those sources and present them to the Trial Chamber. Save for those interviews with the refugees, what other sources did you use?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I draw the court's attention to a full accounting on the narrative titled "Reporting Responsibilities and Sources." Running from page 13 -- paragraph 13 to 16. Those were my sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, among those, are there any sources of knowledge for the specific claims that you are making, and if there are such sources, who are they? Can we check them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Two thing, Dr. Karadzic, first of all I'm not sure it's correct to say that the witness is making specific claims as opposed to reportage. And, secondly, the sources are set out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Second question, who was it who expected you to report things within such a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the United Nations peacekeeping operations. We explained its organisation at the beginning of the narrative headed by General Nambiar who was advised by Mr. Cedric Thornberry as the senior-most civilian at headquarters. On the ground on the designated places known as sectors, a similar arrangement obtained there where there was a sector commander, a military official reporting to General Nambiar, and a civilian official. In Sector North, I was that official, reporting to Cedric Thornberry at the headquarters. Both Cedric and Nambiar reported to the Secretary-General straight through the peacekeeping Undersecretary-General at the time was Marrack Goulding. That chain was a well-defined chain and required those kind of reporting requirements that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So your immediate superior, Mr. Cedric Thornberry expected that from you; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, let's look at what you said in the Milosevic case on the 3rd of February, 2003. On page 15431 you said that Cedric Thornberry sent you a message not to get involved in what was going on in Bosanski Novi because the mandate of the Security Council does not extend over the border; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and it's repeated in this narrative. I forget the exact paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps 61. No, no, 61 is something entirely different. And then in the Brdjanin case you said on page 1415 [as interpreted] that your superiors did not take your reports seriously, and then you used the term "concentration camps" and it was only then that they started taking you seriously; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The word "concentration camp" got their attention, as I explained earlier today, when that entire memo got leaked to the press, appeared in radio stations and TV stations, and the matter was referred to the Security Council. At that moment, Marrack Goulding had to take a plane to Topusko to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you said in paragraph 74 what concentration camps you had in mind, and you mentioned Keraterm, Trnopolje. You said that that was a refugee camp for women, children, and old men, and you also mentioned Omarska and Manjaca. According to you, were those concentration camps?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the people who told us of their existence characterised them as indicated over there in the memo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be reasonable to assume that Cedric Thornberry received from you and from your peers on the ground more information, that he had more information than you had and that the first in the chain of command General Nambiar had even more information than either you or Cedric Thornberry or the both of you together?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can assume that in the nature of logic, but you'd have to qualify it not in every instance. They were receiving it from the ground up, so logically, Dr. Karadzic, you could say the sum total of what they received is greater than those of us who were reporting on specified issues. It won't be true that he knew more about a specified issue. He receives a condensed amount on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you have just repeated what you already stated in the Brdjanin case on 1416 [as interpreted] and that is that General Nambiar opposed the use of the term "concentration camps" and suggested that you should use the term "detention camps"; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm really sorry to interrupt but the Brdjanin transcript, this reference he just gave and the one before or only four digits, and I need five digits, please. Again, I apologise for interrupting but I need the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We all do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have spoken too fast. The page number is 14616. I apologise, 14493.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while you are searching for that, Ms. Sutherland, Dr. Kirudja, isn't it true that you never visited any of those camps, the prisons, detention units, and that you made your inferences based on what people told you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 61 of your statement you speak about your message sent to Mr. Thornberry on the 5th of June and you said that two people who had fled Bosanski Novi described an attack by the local Serbs according to the men, the police then removed the villagers to a football field while their houses were searched and that subsequently their homes were shelled by cannons and mortars from neighbouring Serb villages. And so on and so forth. Can you see the paragraph, 61?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What are the names of the two men who told you all that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have those names but, as you'll see, there are other names that are given whenever I speak of an incident like this. I suspect the reason why those names were never peddled in papers was for their protection because of the subject they were talking about. I remember some people reporting to our civil police, in Dvor particularly, and after they talked to us, they disappeared, and the civil police, which is the custodian of those reports now began to be more guarded about disclosing certain people. I'm not sure that's what happened, but I note that, uncharacteristic of my testimony, those names are not given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I put to you that a few days ago a Muslim from those villages testified and he said that they spent three days in the stadium, that most were released to go home and that even 17 days after that when they left those villages, their houses remained intact. How does that tally with what you are reporting and that is that their houses were shelled while they were still at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see very much difficulty in that. It's entirely possible that some houses could remain standing while others are being shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Dr. Kirudja, the witness said that all the houses were intact when they left their village, but let's leave that, you don't have to know that. But tell us this: How did the two Muslims communicate to you? In what language?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like all people who communicated to me in that area, they spoke their local language and the interpreters interpreted what they said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some of these things happened so long long time ago when there was no issue even when I'm trying not to forget, I do forget if there was no issue. We had a lot of interpreters. With all due respect to them, and I don't remember them so easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karadzic is putting facts to the witness which aren't correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think he left that area but that's been noted in any event.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, when you testified in the Milosevic case, in President Milosevic case on page 15611, did you accept that all the sides to the conflict tended to exaggerate on many things, if not all of the things that they communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a vague memory that is an accurate characterisation, though I don't know exact context that it was made. But it's true, there was a lot of exaggeration on all sides and goes to the question that was asked earlier, do you try to corroborate, to check, to cross-check because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Kirudja, I am afraid that your attitude is someone asymmetrical towards the sides to the conflicts. Look at paragraph 62 where you say that the alleged murders of several Serb members of the Territorial Defence by Muslims and then you say that the alleged massacre in the village of Corkovaca. What I'm trying to say is that when it comes to Serb victims you tends to use the word "allegedly". Whenever Muslim speaks about his or her suffering, you don't use the word "allegedly"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say it does look like that, the paragraph does open itself to that interpretation. I'd like to take just a second to bring an understanding to the court about this. We are not talking about Bosnia in this paragraph. We are talking about the UNPA. We have explained that our mandate required that we observe authorities who had control of the area. The control of that area where this paragraph refers to were the Serb authorities. Now they come with an allegation but wouldn't provide at the request any evidence, and they are the authorities. The difference which Mr. Karadzic correctly observed is that that is not the same thing if you are talking about the minorities who are fleeing, they are not the authorities. And they are telling themselves the story, this is a story being told by the authorities. And if they don't provide any evidence, if people are killed, I can assure you we would go to the scene of the crime very easily. They didn't do it. So the choice for me was to hear a story and not report it, or report it in the context I heard that I have no more information than what the paragraph carries. And in the end, the paragraph, I admit, opens itself to what Dr. Karadzic characterises it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that in the Milosevic case on the 4th of February, 2003, on page 15571 you said, I'll quote: [In English] [As read] "Regardless of whether we had a mandate, we have a model responsibility of having the world hear the story told to us by numerous people who are fleeing from this part of Bosnia." [Interpretation] Did you indeed say so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on paragraph 92 of the narrative, the same thing is repeated almost verbatim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, however, that the attention of the world did not have in mind who reported this, but who signed such a document and they didn't mind or bother to check whether this was a one-sided story or something that was indeed verified?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What document, Dr. Karadzic, are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I was referring to your statement in the Milosevic case where you said that irrespective of the mandate you had a moral obligation or responsibility to report about what Bosnian refugees were telling you. Therefore, I'm asking you this: Such stories which were not verified and which were one-sided is something that was reported to the world, but the world didn't bother to check whether there was any verification, they simply took it all in as if everything had been verified and confirmed.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number one, Dr. Karadzic, I do not, of course, accept that my story was one-sided. And, number two, it wasn't as you say unsigned because you, yourself, can identify to said it and so does anyone who looks at the same statement. They would know the context in which the statement was made, i.e., the trial of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't sufficiently clear, Dr. Kirudja, I'm trying to say this: Conveying one-sided statements made by Muslim refugees on your part caused a lot of damage to us because the world public only -- was only interested in who signed such a report and not who reported it originally. You did not mention alleged crimes, you simply omitted that word and portrayed the crimes as if something that had been verified and accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's a statement, not a question, Dr. Karadzic. And, Dr. Kirudja, when you made your original reports who were they for? Were they internal UN reports or were they for the press?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were internal UN reports which the Prosecutor had to get special authority to access.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But your superiors did not take such internal reports for granted, as you confirmed today. This includes both Mr. Nambiar and Thornberry, who both had their objections to such reporting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a mischaracterisation of what I said to say Dr. -- Mr. Nambiar objected to what I said. He called me to seek clarification what was meant by the word "concentration". I remember very clearly this matter. And it came up again in the Milosevic trial. I think some even played a video of it. Mr. Nambiar was trying to assert in the context in which the word was used and then the word came up, wouldn't it be more appropriate if you used the word "detention," and like I've explained the Court, I mentioned to him, this is not me talking. This is the story of those who have suffered. That's what they call it. Days later, pictures of emaciated prisoners began to hit the press. Now, Dr. Karadzic, what the press says about me or you, for that matter, is something you have absolutely to understand that is what they do the way they do. You don't tell them how to tell the story once they got it. And I'm sure might just have been written by the press. They were not given this information the way Dr. Karadzic may have implied. The world was not given that information that way. This information remained internal information of the United Nations until the Prosecutor got ahold of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, if I told you that the photograph you referred to which cost us a great deal of bombs and suffering was taken in Trnopolje, which you termed refugee camp, what would you say then? Was the photograph implying that it was a concentration camp, although you, yourself, referred to it as a refugee camp? Can you see how two pieces which are untrue have an enormous impact on world public?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This whole statement, Dr. Karadzic, is itself not correct. One, I didn't refer to a photograph myself. Two days later something appeared. It wasn't a photograph that in any way can be associated with my testimony. Number two, I termed it a refugee camp, no. The evidence here doesn't use that word. And, lastly, I am not aware of the link between what may have happened and this event that Dr. Karadzic is piecing together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Kirudja, look at paragraph 74. Following Keraterm you refer to Trnopolje: [In English] "A refugee for women, children, and old men." [Interpretation] The Bench could see for themselves what that camp was like, where people could leave and come in as they wished to procure food. It is in that refugee camp that the photograph was taken and you were not prompted by me, you referred to it yourself.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Karadzic is mischaracterising the evidence. Some people, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it seems to me, I speak for myself alone, fairly fruitless to associate the photograph directly with this witness. He simply referred to it in passing. It's not a photograph that he took or adopted or in any way utilised.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, with all due respect, I believe the witness mentioned the photograph as something he relied on to corroborate what he stated in his report. And, two, wrongful reporting created this situation which the Serb people suffered greatly. Let's drop that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In any case, is it correct, Dr. Kirudja, that you said that in the former Yugoslavia, throughout the former Yugoslavia, you never felt any discrimination against you, and you stated so at page 15489 of your testimony in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, but specifically doesn't say the former Yugoslavia, it says in the area where I was located, and it's an area predominantly controlled by the Serbs. I felt very comfortable, very at ease, and made a lot of friends. I repeat that today; I've always felt that way. Never any such feelings of being discriminated when I lived and worked among the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that in conversation with UN representatives, I officially preferred Asian and African troops as opposed to NATO country troops? We asked that African and Asian soldiers be sent in. Have you ever come across that in any reports?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very, very aware, and this is a sensitive matter for me because I am from the region you are describing, and two battalions of African troops were located in my sector, Sector North. It wasn't a unanimous preference for them, I must say. Though from the Serb side, I can corroborate, never heard what Dr. Karadzic said before, but I had heard it from similar sentiment expressed by other Serbs in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to direct your attention at paragraph 64 of your statement. You mentioned today that your teams were stopped by armed people in Bihac. Do you know who controlled Bihac throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an open-ended statement "throughout the war." I only know the period I was there, who I was dealing with and the extent of their authority while I was dealing with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at paragraph 64 where you say that you reported your Zagreb HQ about the humanitarian disaster unfolding in Bihac and along the Bosnian border. You say you wanted to highlight as clearly as you could to headquarters the urgent need for a humanitarian operation for the Bihac area, and so on and so forth: [In English] [As read] "And I expressed my fear that behind the border the mountains and the forests unspeakable atrocities may be unfolded. The stories coming from Bihac and the surrounding Bosnian municipalities of Velika Kladusa, Cazin, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Krupa, painted a gloomy picture similar to the one unfolding in and around Sarajevo and Mostar at the same time." [Interpretation] A bit further down: [In English] "Additionally, I noticed that in my opinion Serb stories of atrocities committed by Muslims such as axing to death of 40 Serbs in a two-day period were part of a concerted effort by Serbian leaders on both sides of the border to paint the Muslims in the area as dangerous." [Interpretation] Dr. Kirudja, do you know that Serbs had no access whatsoever to Velika Kladusa and Cazin, and that if there were atrocities committed there, they could only have been committed among the Muslims themselves in their internal clashes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true. That's an area I lived, worked, and observed firsthand. We had a lot of fighting in there. I'm thinking even one example, some groups of Serbs from the UNPA led by one Colonel Isaac [phoen] woke up one afternoon and went into Bosnia and took up a big enclave of it and wouldn't come out, until we found a way to end that fighting. Later because of -- it was a very unique area where there were four-way conflict unlike elsewhere in Bosnia. There were conflicts between Serbs and the Croats, that were conflicts between Serbs and Muslims, and there were conflicts between Muslims versus Muslims in the area. It was a very hectic area. A lot of things were going on. No, it's not true to say nothing happened there. Plenty happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this: Are you accusing Bosnian Serbs, people from my country which I presided over, to have entered Kladusa, Cazin, and Bihac in order to commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I notice now you have changed a little bit because the paragraph was talking about Serbs, when you started out, Dr. Karadzic. I hear you now talking about people from your country and I assume it's the rest of Bosnia. No, I never reported about that, nor would I be reporting since I wouldn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And yet you believed that atrocities were committed over Serbs in the Bihac pocket; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not I believed, I reported about that, what was going on there. We held numerous peace and reconciliation meetings between the people who were fighting in there on a day-to-day basis. It wasn't a belief, it was a report of what was going on while we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the 5th Corps of the Army of BH, which was stationed in Bihac, was a powerful military formation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I met with its commander severally. It was, as you characterise it, a powerful force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that in the war between Muslims and Muslims, Serbs sided with Fikret Abdic, whom they saw as a pro-European Muslim?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several rounds of fightings and it would be incorrect except towards the end to characterise which side the Serbs associated with in the earlier fightings. In the end the two groups did split on the 5th Corps of Bihac and fought each other, with Abdic on one side, and what we called the Sarajevo-supported group on the other side. The Sarajevo-supported group won.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that I signed a peace agreement with Mr. Abdic early on in the war, sometime in 1993, and that the fighting between our troops and Abdic's stopped?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had extensive discussions with Fikret Abdic and part of that was involving what he said he signed with Mr. Karadzic, Dr. Karadzic. Yes, I am aware, because I spoke at length with Fikret Abdic about those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 65 you discuss 200 people, or even 850 who had arrived from Sanski Most. Did you know that those people from Sanski Most, that brigade, had taken seven of our soldiers prisoner in order to blackmail us so that we would let them pass through and provide our own buses for their transport to the Bihac pocket. We saw such documents here already, I just wanted to know for the time being whether you were aware of that. They asked us to let them through to the Bihac pocket aboard our buses and that these were hardened fighters we had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. They characterised Manjaca as a concentration camp, as we can see in paragraph 65; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They meaning the group referred to in paragraph 65 -- 65?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I understood that correctly.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so because the content of paragraph 74 I had already apprised the Court that were done in our office following the night of a huge number of refugees. So if some of them had been part of that group, I wouldn't be able to tell. It's entirely possible. But they were not a fighting force. It's a group of refugees when they arrived and before they could be escorted out, we needed to debrief them, so we understand what is going on and why they were running away from whatever they were running away from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 53 you discuss Mr. Kupresanin having called the civil affairs office in Sector North and spoke to Paolo Raffone and he asked that the local authorities be helped to protect the Muslim population in the municipalities of Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, Kljuc, Dubica, Sanski Most and Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes further down: [In English] "He also appealed to the UNPROFOR and western countries to find a way to protect the civilian Muslim population." [Interpretation] Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Kupresanin was asked by me to visit Manjaca and the Muslim villages there and that he was the highest representative of the ARK authorities, he was the Assembly speaker of the ARK until it ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Mr. Kupresanin was the first person to appear on the ballot list of the SDS on the electoral unit of Banja Luka when the votes were being cast to the republican parliament in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that when you provide your assessments of the SDS, it would be useful for you to know what position Mr. Kupresanin had and on whose behalf he undertook these humanitarian efforts? Would it not be quite appropriate for you to know he was the person number one in the civilian authorities of the ARK?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We made every effort to know who it is we were talking to and who they represented and what is it they wanted. We ask as much -- as many questions to enable us to understand the situation. It doesn't mean we got answers. It doesn't mean if I had asked him, are you working with Dr. Karadzic he would have said yes. In those situations, it took a long time for people to understand who the interlocutors were. And lastly, he had made a telephone call to my office. Telephone calls, as you would know, are not your best way of disclosure and saying who you are to -- you never know exactly who is at the other end of the line. But he had an important message about the refugees and that was heard and recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: We'll take a break now for a quarter of an hour. Dr. Karadzic, although there is time available, you've had over an hour more than the time that was originally assessed as appropriate, so if you could finish your cross-examination within and before the allotted time, no doubt that would be appreciated by all. Not the least the witness who has had a very long day. We'll rise for a quarter of an hour now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, let's clarify one thing. You did not doubt the fact that Mr. Kupresanin was an official, that he was a politician and that he was in power there; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason to do that given the subject he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about Raffone, did he not believe that he was mayor of Banja Luka? You spoke about that in the Brdjanin case on the 10th of February, page 14592.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on it became clear he wasn't -- he was later identified as not the mayor of Banja Luka. Mr. Raffone, I repeat, was talking to him on the telephone with an interpreter. You know the complications of talking to someone on the telephone with an interpreter, a lot could be misunderstood, and it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Kirudja, does it make a difference if a citizen calls you or the call is from a high official since you claim that he was not the mayor? Did you not find it important to establish who Kupresanin was?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Mr. Raffone undertook this job on my behalf. He comes to the office with the information, he prepares a note, I debrief him and when I'm clear what it is, I sign a release for that information. I didn't doubt that he asked all the questions that he needed to ask to authenticate who it is that was speaking to him and making the request that he was making. Besides, he was quite an experienced civil affairs officer and he did his job very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to go back to my main point. Did you not find it important that you were called by the highest political leader in Bosnia and Herzegovina and asked you to protect the Muslims? Did you not think that that was an important fact that should have been taken into account?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier I doubted that he identified himself as your highest representative in that area. He just talked about the refugees, the fact that he was being mistaken in his role is -- speaks for itself. I can assure you had he said I'm speaking on behalf of Dr. Karadzic, a red flag would have gone up. Wherever I was, I would have been called to take care of this information. Maybe it's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, why didn't you take interest in who it who was calling and asking you for help? If you had found out that he was the highest political authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina, wouldn't that have made a difference for you when passing judgement on the SDS? How come you overlooked that fact when you were making your decisions and judgements about the situation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you are terribly mistaken that I didn't take interest. The fact that I assigned somebody else to deal with this issue is because on a single day I couldn't do everything as head of that office. And I have delegated responsibilities. Yes, I knew what was the matter because that staff knew enough to come and brief me. It doesn't follow I took no interest. Actually, I did take plenty of interest in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you took interest in Mr. Kupresanin's position and why he was calling you to ask your assistance, on behalf of what authority? Did you investigate that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently, Dr. Karadzic, you are talking about this relationship to you and how big it was. I'm talking about the substance he was talking about: 15.000 persons. Any time you -- anyone would call and say there is that many people in that situation, that was our job. Already even if there were two or three, we would pay attention; this is 15.000. That's the nature of the interest, not the fact that he was your highest representative. We didn't know that, with all due respect, so we couldn't take interest on account that he was your highest representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But with all due respect, Dr. Kirudja, in paragraph 111 you did notice that Vlado Vrkes was the president of a small Municipal Board. At the same time you did not notice that he was the president of the parliament of the Autonomous Province of Krajina, a very high political official, and that makes me think that you were selective and very partial because you knew exactly who the president of a small Municipal Board was and that was a much lower position than the position that Dr. Kupresanin held at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guarantee you, Dr. Karadzic, if he had characterised himself the way you are characterising him, a big point would have made of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the witness has asked and answered these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, and I think the last answer I think should suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's move on then. What did you understand about those 15.000 men? Where did you think that they came from? Did you think that they came from those municipalities that he mentioned to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement amended in the paragraph is the reason why interest first and foremost, I'll read it: [As read] "He estimated that approximately 15.000 persons had already left their usual place of residence and had started moving towards Dvor." Dvor was the UNPA, this was within our day-to-day responsibility. Being informed that 15.000 people headed your way was enough to get our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But didn't you think that they were all from Bosanski Novi but rather from Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, Kljuc, Dubica Sanski Most and Banja Luka, I'm talking about these 15.000 people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made as much effort to ascertain where they were coming from. To put this in context earlier than this date we had 4.000 people said to be passing through the centre -- through the UNPA. They turned out to be 9.000 and it was a huge operation lasting until midnight at night. To be informed that three times that number is headed your way, whether it turned out to be true or not, that was significant. That's why I'm saying to the Court, we paid attention; very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we now look at 1D4844.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for the document can you tell us if you that in your reports reported on discords and conflicts between Belgrade and Pale, more precisely about the attempts on the part of President Milosevic to overthrow those in power in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some reports covering that subject, though the word "overthrow," it's the first time I'm hearing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]Can we look at the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature or rather is this the cover letter that you sent together with your associate's memorandum? Is it true that the allegations about the arrest and remanding in custody of the 42 Muslims in the school were checked by you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the bottom of this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to stay on this where you say: [In English] "The fear of the presence of enemies in the area was mitigated by the fact that the local authorities were visibly walking around without any special direction."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here you say that CIVPOL and POLBAT expressed their satisfaction with the results and hoped to repeat this kind of co-operation. When it comes to the stories on the arrest of 42 Muslims did you check those stories and did you find them not to be true?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area, Your Honour, referred to in the memo is inside the UNPA and is about a half an hour's drive from my office, was under the battalion from Poland. It was easy to access, it was easy to check what was going on. So yes, this story wouldn't have been one of those challenging ones to cover in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Unlike this time when you checked, are you saying that you did not have an occasion to travel to Bosnia to cross the border and check similar stories there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia, the stories came to me even if I wasn't looking for them by virtue of the people who crossed over. The difference between a story taking place in Slunj where this report took place, this is an area we all day go around doing what the Vance Plan requested us to do. Bosnia on the other hand, we haven't been through this before. There was no UN mandate in Bosnia, so it's not even an unwillingness to cross over there. If you are in charge of UN assets, you don't deploy them where you have no mandate, but the stories came to you because the effect of what was going on couldn't be prevented from coming to you. So that is the distinction. Not the fact that there was an unwillingness to go there or even that inability of the logistics; we had car, we had planes, we had all of that. You can't deploy them except where the mandate requires them to be deployed. This was within the mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1919, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at 65 ter 6757.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, just briefly if we can, please look at the document and just briefly confirm for us that this is indeed your report? 8 October 1992, your report; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise that as my signature covering a report. This is the cover to a report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in paragraph 4 at the end you claim that the Croatian government objected to the opening of borders for the Muslim refugees, and then in paragraph 5 you say that Muslims were resorting to very bold attempts to lift the blockade and cross the territory that you were responsible of; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's another paragraph on the second page to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, 5. Paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the paragraph talks about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now can we see the bottom part of the page. Do you say in paragraph 8 that most of the destabilizing activities or events along the Cazinska Krajina stem from attempts by Muslims trapped in that enclave to break out at all cost; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then under (a) you mention two cases of infiltration. Look at (b) where you establish that the Muslims were engaged in the ethnical cleansing of an area north of the rivers Prosinja and Bonja on the border with Serbian Krajina and you say that of the original Serb population of more than 28.000 Serbs living in Cazinska Krajina, less than 7.000 are reported as still living in the Muslim enclave. That was in October 1992. Up to then, the 21.000 mentioned in here had already been cleansed; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again the court should kindly place the occurrence of this event inside the UNPA, again with a different understanding of what these reports were about. We are no longer talking about events across the border. We are talking about events inside. The infiltration is to inside the UNPA. The absence of any number of ethnic groups in there was already a fact before the UNPA. That area had been cleansed of mostly Croats in the UNPA, but also of some Muslims. So to understand this report is to where the Vance Plan mandate to understand what this report was about. It's different from what was going on across the border with people coming from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Muslims and from other parts of Bosnia and Serbs from the Bihac pocket arrived in your area; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at paragraphs (c) and (d), where you say: "Military fortification of the Muslim stronghold. Serb authorities claim that Cazinska Krajina is being supplied militarily by air through a landing strip in Cazin." Then under (d), you say that the Muslim commanders readily welcome Muslim prisoners released by Serbs because they are then mobilised again; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can we look at paragraph 10 where you say that up to then, Serbs in UNPA zones tolerated Muslim refugees, but the question is how long is that going to last. That's at the end of paragraph 10; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Again you are probably going to begin to understand an earlier comment that I made that that was the area with the most complicated four-way fightings. Serbs, Muslims, Croats, and Muslims versus Muslims. This report begins to address because it was necessary for me to file reports covering the entire mandate of the UN, so this was beginning to tell them this area is beginning to take this shape. Vance Plan required the status quo be held before the solution would come from [indiscernible] in Geneva. People were not supposed -- whether they were Muslim, Serbs or Croats, to be moved from where they were. The agreement in Belgrade and in Zagreb was everybody was to stay where they are and if possible people should return where they came from. This report begins now to address those issues. So I would like Dr. Karadzic to be aware of when something was happening inside the UNPA and a reportage of the same, it had different dimensions of informing, clarifying, and forewarning what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Five more minutes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can the document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja, can you please confirm whether these are things that you observed and described as happening in your UNPA zone? There were Muslim and Serb refugees and can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do so authenticate this report as one of my reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am sorry. Just on that last document that Your Honour asked me if I had any objection and I said that I didn't and that was admitted as D1919. I didn't object because it was authored by the witness but it's simply not relevant to this indictment. It's in the UNPA and the passages were read into the record that Dr. Karadzic wanted to put to the witness, so I think it's -- I should have objected at the time and I'm sorry I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I don't think there's anything lost. As with all documents, its admission and weight of course are two separate considerations.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the current document is Exhibit P3860, part of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 1D4841. I apologise, our team is very small, it's very hard for me to follow things and I don't want to waste time on the documents that have already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is also your signature and this is also one of your documents; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a cover to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go immediately to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you report that in your zone there are 15.000 Serb refugees and displaced persons, that they are accommodated in their relative's houses and in the houses of their friends?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, this document, again, is about the UNPA. The reference is the protection of minorities who were there before we entered and they could have been any minority, whether they were Croat or Muslims. So as long as you understand this also is in the same category as the other document, the issues being discussed are within the Vance Plan, within the UNPA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Dr. Kirudja, the 15.000 refugees were refugees from Bosnia, obviously. The process was over there and peace was already established there; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says so in paragraph 26 over there where they say those 15.000 refugees live in Sector North and they already taken refuge there. Vance Plan required that no movement be made, status quo be maintained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And come to your last question, please, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has spoken to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1920, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last document then. I would like to ask you to tell us whether the documents you were so kind to review are authentic. Could we next have 65 ter 5168.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is your report. On page 1 we have the Serb-Muslim segment where you discuss medical evacuation and humanitarian convoys which regularly traversed the sector. And they went across the crossing points that are specified.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page so that you can have a look, and then on page 3 we have the all-Serb border segment. Do you agree that the Serbs who were on both sides of the river could not have been interested in destroying the bridge connecting them?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What paragraph is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 9. It discusses your awareness that Serbs live on both sides of the river in Bosanska Kostajnica and Hrvatska Kostajnica, as well as, Dorno Uni [phoen] and Bosanski Novi. Do you agree that when Serbs are on both sides of the river, they are not interested in destroying the bridge; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number one, Your Honour, there were more than one bridge along that segment that we are discussing. Number two, yes, I would to a limited extent expect what Dr. Karadzic said to be true, but only to a limited extent. The only time you can recognise that won't be true is if the Croats had attacked, which they eventually did from their side, that won't be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that looking at the time that must be it, and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I wanted to refer you to line 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you receive information that there was ethnic cleansing in Bosanska Dubica when the Muslims themselves specified some municipalities including Dubica in which ethnic cleansing did not occur?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see paragraph 6, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think it was line 6 rather than paragraph 6, Dr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, in this document. Paragraph 9, line 6. Was this also based on refugee stories or did you have some other insight or proof?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of people moving across that border. One group I vividly remember had crossed from Dubica. I was called by the Danish military and all the military observers that covered that area that this group of people were surrounded by Serb who demanded that they don't move from there and they were in danger of being mis-characterised not as refugees but as terrorists. That -- when we went there we found them and began to debrief them, where they were coming from. And we developed that that area was also being cleared of non-Serbs from their testimony. The Serb authorities were quite co-operative in not demanding that they put them in prison but by releasing them for custody with the civil affairs and sending them out. Yes, many of those stories came from people who had the stories to tell. And, lastly, while we could not deploy either the soldiers or the UN civil police across the border to Dubica, we had an agreement with both sides to deploy military observers. These are not formed units. These are individual military observers who [indiscernible] that area. So both sides of these border segments, whether it was controlled by the Serbs on both sides or not, we had military observers on that side. And we had NGOs and we had European monitoring, all the sources that were mentioned in the paragraphs that I drew the court's attention, taking them together, we could piece together what was going on, where these people were coming from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sutherland, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Over the break, I read the transcript and it's very clear. Sorry, there's no need for any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, there's just one housekeeping matter, Exhibit 65 ter 06732 that the Prosecutor had indicated was part of Exhibit D470 but the Registry advises us that it's not so I would tender that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, I was informed about that, so that can be exhibited under a separate number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1921, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since there is no redirect, I just wanted to ask Dr. Kirudja whether he believed that Serbs from one side of the river drove Muslims out without notifying the Serbs on the other side of the river? How could you accept what they told you when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the Court has ruled and you've been given a huge amount of leeway with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for my own understanding of the disposition of some, one document that I was given to review by Dr. Karadzic's side, and I could ask the Courts to consider this document dated 29 of April 1995 is among the document, it's a very personal and confidential document. Has nothing to do with anything in the criminal trial and I wondered whether the Court would expunge it from this document. It's a personal document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I don't think that's been tendered. Certainly not as far as I am aware before the court. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it would be helpful to explain to the witness that although he was asked to review documents -- I presume this is one of the documents he was asked to review during the lunch break, although he was asked to review documents, the only documents tendered into evidence are the ones that were actually presented to him subsequently in court, so the fact that he reviewed the document doesn't mean that that document is entered the evidence base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I hope that reassures you, Dr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like the same assurance that the source who gave me, Dr. Karadzic, that this document is a purely personal document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think you can rely on Dr. Karadzic to honour that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Kirudja, thank you very much for attending and giving evidence before us, particularly, thank you for bearing with what is a very extended day. I thank the interpreters and all staff and indeed everybody for their indulgence as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Swahili spoken] I'm glad you could say that. It makes me feel a little at home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you, we'll all rise. Thank you, we sit again, I believe next Wednesday at 1.00. 12.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of November, 2011, at 12.00 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
